items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Rhetoric and Communication. Interdisciplinary Studies in the Humanities The intersection of Rhetoric and Communication continues to attract the interest of many scholars, particularly within the fields of the Humanities and Social Sciences. The scope of analysis is wide-ranging, encompassing literature and culture, language studies and advertising, communication studies and politics, among other domains. In this Volume, we aim to bring together a set of studies that focus directly on topics shared by Rhetoric and Communication, from Classical Antiquity to the present, from an interdisciplinary perspective. Scholarly contributions across the Humanities will enhance our understanding of the influence of rhetoric and communication on society, taking into account, on the one hand, there is a vast legacy that merits further study and, on the other, new forms of communication require us to reassess the impact of the rhetorical art. This Volume welcomes contributions of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, from within the field of the Humanities. Possible topics include: · Rhetorical and communication theory applied to discourse; · Treatises on rhetoric and communication; · The presence of rhetorical genres in contemporary forms of communication; · Argumentation techniques and persuasion in literary texts, the media, advertising, or other narrative forms; · The contemporary relevance of teaching rhetoric and communication; · The contemporary application of classical rhetoric in the media; · Rhetoric in political discourse and in literary composition; · Philosophical perspectives on rhetoric and communication; · The role of the audience and the addressee in rhetorical theory and in the communicative process; · Representations of rhetoric and communication in the Arts. Editors: Cristina Santos Pinheiro, Joaquim Pinheiro, Rui Carlos Fonseca, Samuel Mateus, Telmo Reis e Vanessa Cesário Proposals, in Word format, should be submitted by 10 September 2026 to the following email address: retorica.comunicacao@mail.uma.pt The Volume is scheduled for publication in March 2027 by a leading national publisher. All submissions will be subject to scientific evaluation (blind peer review). Authors will be notified of the review decision by 30 November 2026. 1. Accepted languages Submissions will be accepted in Portuguese, French, English, and Spanish. 2. Formatting guidelines 2.1. Length and formatting: main text: maximum of 20 A4 pages and minimum of 12 A4 pages; font: 11 pt, Aptos, 1.5 line spacing; footnotes: 10 pt, Aptos, single spacing. 2.2. Title centred, 12 pt, bold, Aptos. 2.3. Author name(s), affiliation (University, Institute, Research Unit or equivalent), email address, and ORCID should be provided in 11 pt, Aptos. 2.4. Two abstracts (maximum 250 words each) must be included: one in the language of the article and one in English, followed by up to five keywords. 3. General guidelines 3.1. Citations and references should follow APA style (7th ed.); all citations must be properly identified. 3.2. Quotations longer than three lines must be indented 1 cm from the left margin. 3.3. a) Italics should be used for the titles of works, modern monographs, and journals. b) Quotation marks (" ") should be used for quotations from modern texts. c) Italics should not be used for Latin abbreviations (op. cit., loc. cit., cf., ibid., in…). 4. Footnotes Footnotes should be brief. 5. Images/Graphs/Tables 5.1. Any graphical elements must be clearly identified and numbered. 5.2. Images must be submitted in .jpeg format, with a minimum resolution of 300 dpi, be free of copyright fees, and accompanied by official proof of permission or purchase of rights for academic publication. Each submission may include no more than four images (printing will not be in color). 6. Final bibliography The bibliography should be limited to essential works or cited references and must conform to APA style (7th ed.). 7. Publication The Volume will be published by a Portuguese publisher with extensive experience in scientific publishing. It will also be made available as an e-book in institutional repositories. 8. Copyright statement Submissions must be original, and authors grant publication rights upon acceptance.

items.fullDescription: This conference explores decay as a transformative, liminal state that bridges the physical, the political, and the conceptual. During the process of decomposition, systems and objects start to break down, existing in a precarious limbo that simultaneously signals contamination to the surrounding environment. As theorized by Julia Kristeva in Powers of Horror, the abject corpse and the decaying material remind us of the fragility of our own boundaries, confronting us with what must be cast off to constitute a stable self. This fear of bodily disintegration and abjection mirrors the anxieties we project onto broader cultural and institutional structures.

items.fullDescription: Affiliated with the British Association for Chinese Studies (BACS), the British Postgraduate Network for Chinese Studies (BPCS) is an academic network for postgraduate students and early-career researchers in Chinese Studies in the UK. With over 1,000 members, BPCS is one of the largest postgraduate organisations for Chinese Studies in the UK. We actively promote Chinese Studies by organising annual conferences, seminars, career events, and other academic and professional activities. We also aim to serve as a key source of information on developments in Chinese Studies across the UK and to give members opportunities to connect with peers in their fields. Available Positions We are currently inviting nominations for three committee positions: President: Provides executive leadership for BPCS activities, including the annual conference, and attends BACS meetings as a representative of the community. Internal Secretary: Works with the President to organise BPCS activities, particularly the annual conference, and assumes the responsibilities of the President in their absence. External Secretary: Edits and publishes the weekly newsletter, manages BPCS social media accounts and external communications, and works with the President and Internal Secretary to promote BPCS events and activities. We warmly invite you to nominate yourself for one of these positions. If you would like to nominate someone else, please feel free to share this email and the link https://forms.gle/4Fp34qN9pbwFnZEGA with them. Application Procedure Members are invited to nominate themselves or other candidates by completing the https://forms.gle/4Fp34qN9pbwFnZEGA by 04 October 2026. A confirmation email will be sent once we have received your nomination. We will finalise the list of nominees for each position shortly after the deadline, followed by an election. The results will be announced through the BPCS mailing list by October 2026, subject to the election results and confirmation from the successful candidates. The newly elected members will take office on 23 October 2026. Why Should You Consider Joining Us? Joining the BPCS Committee offers more than an opportunity to strengthen your professional experience. It allows you to become part of an academic community committed to advancing Chinese Studies in the UK. As a committee member, you will gain valuable networking and organisational experience, have opportunities to develop events related to your academic and professional interests, and contribute to initiatives that benefit the wider Chinese Studies community. Your participation will help ensure the continuation of the BPCS annual conference, newsletters, seminars, and other regular activities. We warmly encourage you to consider joining the BPCS Committee and helping to shape the future of our organisation. Together, we can build a supportive and collaborative community for Chinese Studies. We look forward to receiving your nominations and working together to further the study of Chinese culture and society in the UK.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS Christians and Muslims in Israel - Facts, Myths and Lived Reality International Online Academic Conference 25-28 January 2027 Online via Zoom Working language: English Call for papers for an international online conference on Christianity, Islam, religious minorities, interreligious relations, religious freedom, identity, society and politics in contemporary Israel. The Institute for Hebrew Language and Literature, Belgrade, invites scholars and researchers to submit paper proposals for the international interdisciplinary conference "Christians and Muslims in Israel - Facts, Myths and Lived Reality," to be held online via Zoom from 25 to 28 January 2027. CONFERENCE OVERVIEW The conference will examine the historical, social, religious, demographic, legal, cultural and political realities of Christian and Muslim communities in the State of Israel. Its purpose is to distinguish empirical evidence and lived experience from simplified assumptions, stereotypes and politically driven narratives. Different scholarly interpretations are welcome, and participants are not required to adopt any predetermined political, theological or ideological position. In addition to Christian-Muslim relations, the conference welcomes research on Christians and Muslims as distinct communities and on their relationships with the Jewish majority, the State of Israel, public institutions and wider Israeli society. Relevant disciplinary perspectives include sociology of religion, religious studies, history, theology, anthropology, political science, law, demography, education, Middle Eastern Studies, Israel Studies, minority studies, media studies and related interdisciplinary fields. CONFERENCE TOPICS Proposals may address, but are not limited to: Christians in contemporary Israeli society Muslims in contemporary Israeli society Arab Christian and Arab Muslim communities Christian-Muslim relations in Israel Jewish-Christian relations Jewish-Muslim relations Religious minorities and the State of Israel Religion, government and public policy Religious freedom and the legal status of religious communities Religious institutions, authorities and leadership Education and religious identity Demographic change, migration and religious communities Political and civic participation Jerusalem and its religious communities Sacred spaces, holy places and shared religious sites Discrimination, integration and social mobility Coexistence and interreligious encounters Gender and religion Media representations, stereotypes and public narratives Myths about Christians and Muslims in Israel versus empirical evidence Religion, ethnicity, citizenship and national identity The everyday experiences of Christian and Muslim communities Historical perspectives on Christians and Muslims in Israel Comparative perspectives on religious minorities and interreligious relations The conference is intended for established scholars, early-career researchers, doctoral candidates and other specialists whose work can make a serious academic contribution to the conference theme. SUBMISSION REQUIREMENTS Applicants should submit: First name Last name Institution or academic affiliation Email address Proposed paper title Abstract of no more than 150 words Abstracts and proposed paper titles must be submitted in English. Submit your proposal through the official submission form: https://religion.hebrew.edu.rs/submit-abstract IMPORTANT DATES Conference: 25-28 January 2027 Standard abstract submission deadline: 10 October 2026 Applicants are encouraged to submit their proposals as early as possible to allow sufficient time for academic review and any necessary revisions. Late proposals submitted after 10 October 2026 may be considered subject to the availability of places in the conference programme. SPEAKER PARTICIPATION FEE The participation fee applies only to speakers whose proposed topic and abstract have been formally reviewed and accepted by the Editorial Board. Applicants must not make any payment when submitting an abstract. Payment is required only after the applicant receives written confirmation that the proposed paper has been accepted. Speaker participation fees are: €89 for topics and abstracts submitted by 1 September 2026 €120 for topics and abstracts submitted by 10 October 2026 €189 for topics and abstracts submitted after 10 October 2026 Conference participation fees support the European Hebrew Journal and its continued operation as a Diamond Open Access academic journal. This model helps ensure that scholarly research remains openly available without access barriers. ACADEMIC PUBLICATION Selected papers presented at the conference may be considered for publication in peer-reviewed conference proceedings. Authors of selected papers will have an opportunity to revise their work following academic feedback. CONFERENCE FORMAT The conference will be held entirely online via Zoom, allowing scholars and participants to join from any country. Conference sessions will take place each day between 14:00 and 20:00 CET. Working language: English ORGANISER Institute for Hebrew Language and Literature Belgrade, Serbia https://www.hebrew.edu.rs European Hebrew Journal: https://ehj.hebrew.edu.rs CONFERENCE WEBSITE Full conference information: https://religion.hebrew.edu.rs/current-conference Abstract submission: https://religion.hebrew.edu.rs/submit-abstract Contact: office@hebrew.edu.rs

items.fullDescription: EchoForum 2026 Conference: Disability as Radical Interdisciplinary Practice 26-27 November 2026 Organised by: Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu NEW Submission deadline: 10 October 2026 Working languages: English, French, Romanian Confirmed Keynote Speakers: Jonathan Meth // Goldsmiths University of London Maria Bucur // Indiana University Petra Kuppers // University of Michigan EchoForum: Conceptual Framework Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu and the members of the EchoCamp project are delighted to extend an invitation to the upcoming conference on disability arts, EchoForum 2026: Disability as Radical Interdisciplinary Practice, taking place between November 26-27, 2026 , in Sibiu, Romania. EchoForum constitutes the research and dialogue component of EchoCamp, the first artistic camp dedicated to disability arts in Romania. Paying homage to Camp Jened and to other similar undertakings, EchoCamp aims to radically shape the way in which we think about the intersection of disability, arts, inclusion, and representation in the East-European cultural space. Hence, at its core, the EchoForum conference is conceived as an interdisciplinary crossroad. We believe that disability does not exist in a vacuum, but is shaped by politics of space, care, law, aesthetic frameworks, and broader social organization. Consequently, we seek to move beyond the siloed approach to disability studies, inviting a convergence of knowledge from across the humanities, social sciences, and professional practices. Therefore, we invite contributions that intersect across the following academic and professional domains: The Artistic and Media Humanities: Including Performing Arts, Visual Arts, Film and Media, Literature and Literary Studies, Theatre and Performance Studies, and the field of Artistic Research. The Social and Cultural Sciences: Including Sociology and Social Work, Anthropology, Cultural Studies, Critical Theory, Disability Studies, and the intersectional frameworks of Gender, Sexuality, and Queer Studies. Spatial and Infrastructural Studies: Including Architecture and Spatial Practices, Accessibility and Inclusive Design, and the fields of Curatorial Studies and Cultural Management and Policy. Health and Care Humanities: Including Healthcare/Health Humanities, Psychology, and Education/Pedagogy. Applied Practices and Advocacy: Including Community-based Practice, Political Activism, and Human Rights Advocacy. Since we believe that all knowledge is created equal, we welcome proposals from both academic and non-academic contexts. We invite contributions in a variety of formats: Theoretical and practice-based research (including work-in-progress and case studies). Artistic research and presentations of cultural practices or projects. Interdisciplinary panels and roundtable discussions. Hybrid formats, such as performance-lectures or workshops. We invite both individual and collective proposals. Abstracts may be submitted in English, French, or Romanian. However, presentations may be delivered only in English or Romanian. As a general guideline for programming and scheduling, we suggest a duration of 20 minutes for individual presentations. However, we emphasize that this timeframe is a suggestion and not a strict requirement. In alignment with our commitment to accessibility and inclusive practice, we recognize that different modes of communication, the use of assistive technologies, and various cognitive or physical needs may require alternative timing or pacing. We encourage applicants to propose a duration and format that best ensures their ability to present their work comfortably and effectively. Submit your proposal via the following online form: https://forms.gle/pyVsovHeu3yDkpDeA Practical Information Dates: 26-27 November 2026 Deadline: 10 October 2026 Notification of Acceptance: 15 October 2026 Venue: Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Sibiu, Romania Fees: No registration fee. Access: EchoCamp is committed to full accessibility. Please detail your requirements in the application form. EchoFestival: The Forum is followed by EchoFestival, the public programme featuring performances and artistic events. Selected contributors are warmly invited to stay and participate. Contact For questions or support with the application: echocamp2026@gmail.com We're looking forward to welcoming you to Sibiu! EchoForum is committed to accessibility in all its dimensions. We prioritize the voices of disabled artists, researchers, and practitioners and welcome your feedback on how to make this Forum truly inclusive.

items.fullDescription: From its founding ideals framing rights as tied to individuals to many of the ‘myths that made America,’ such as the self-made man, ideas of individualism are deeply entrenched in the culture of the United States. Yet at the same time, the US has also always understood itself as a particular community: as a city upon a hill, a melting pot, a more perfect union. As such, the United States has been established on a seeming paradox, forming ‘out of many, one.’ More recently, this previous consensus has become increasingly brittle, with fragmentation, polarization, hyper-individualism, and loneliness on the rise—as some would argue: again.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PRESENTATION PAPER ABSTRACTS "Are Karl Marx's 'Perpetuum Mobile' and/or Max Weber's 'Machine State' Dominating Labor Today? Why or Why Not?" Students, researchers, faculty members, and scholars working in sociology and related social sciences are invited to submit conference presentation paper abstracts for an open conference session entitled "Are Karl Marx's 'Perpetuum Mobile' and/or Max Weber's 'Machine State' Dominating Labor Today? Why or Why Not?" The session will be part of the XXI International Sociological Association (ISA) World Congress of Sociology, from July 4-10, 2027, at Chonnam National University in Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City, Korea. Karl Marx and Max Weber both thought about a time when machines would dominate labor. Marx wrote of a "perpetuum mobile" to describe the unceasing turnover of money by a machine of indestructible materiality, circulating a repeating and alternating flow of sale and purchase. Max Weber's "Sociology of Domination" theory warned that the power to coerce markets endlessly would cause endless conflicts. For Marx social change entailed communist revolution, while Weber, who was not a Marxist, worried that social change would be constricted to political coups to control the government's informational infrastructure. Social problems of alienation and rationalization, capitalist wealth and inequality, abuse of power and authority, coerced markets, money hording and social stratification are as alive today as when Marx and Weber set down theories about these social problems over a hundred years ago. What can we say about our AI dominated world using the concepts and writings of Marx and Weber today? Do their economic and historical comparative concepts help us understand our digital world? Why or why not? Submit presentation abstracts by October 14, 2026, through the ISA Congress Submission System link below. ISA XXI World Congress of Sociology Call for Abstracts: https://www.isa-sociology.org/isa-events/xxi-world-congress-of-sociology/call-for-abstracts Watch the 2025 ISA abstract submission tutorial here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p_dRzY4k_o4 Current Session Participants: Session Chair, Dr. Ece Kocabicak, The Open University Co-Chair, Dr. Pravat Ranjan Sethi, Central University of Himachal Pradesh, India Discussant, Proshant Chakraborty, University of Vienna, Austria Session Organizer, Dr. Noel Packard, Independent Scholar, USA Questions? Contact Dr. Noel Packard at npac825@aucklanduni.ac.nz. Further information available via Sociology Group interview with Dr. Noel Packard on Marx, Weber, and machines dominating labour: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/414162540_An_Interview_with_Dr_Noel_Packard_- Karl_Marx_and_Max_Weber_on_Machines_Dominating_Labour

items.fullDescription: Despite the international prominence of Stanisław Lem and, more recently, Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher , Polish science fiction and speculative literature remain strikingly underrepresented in English-language scholarship. items.fullDescription: Plastic / Plasticity Literature and Culture and the Material of a (Bygone?) Era Plastic is a defining material of our era. Its properties—plasticity, durability, the ability to imitate any shape, its toxicity, and indecomposability—are also properties of contemporary culture and literature. The proposed thematic issue begins with the premise that plastic can be read simultaneously as a historical substance and as a "theory machine"—a tool for understanding cultural texts and the experience of contemporary times. "My approach, in this paper, is one of thinking with plastic through its metaphoricity and materiality, its relationality and gestationality; in short, a material mediality.” [R. Gosh]

items.fullDescription: Call For Paper Women And Art: Representation, Creativity, And Resistance Open Access | Maurer Press, Frankfurt am Main, Germany Edited by Habib Tekin & Ay?enur Özkan I??k Art has long served as a powerful space in which gender identities, social roles, cultural expectations, and forms of resistance are constructed, questioned, and reimagined. Across different historical periods and cultural contexts, women have participated in artistic production as creators, performers, patrons, critics, and subjects of representation. Yet their contributions have frequently been shaped by unequal access to artistic institutions, dominant aesthetic traditions, and gendered structures of visibility and recognition. The conference "Women and Art: Representation, Creativity, and Resistance" invites scholars, researchers, artists, and postgraduate students to explore the complex and changing relationship between women and artistic production. The conference seeks to bring together interdisciplinary perspectives on how women create, experience, interpret, and transform art, as well as how femininity and gender are represented within different artistic forms. We particularly welcome contributions that examine the ways in which art can function as a space of memory, identity formation, cultural negotiation, political intervention, and resistance. Papers may address historical or contemporary contexts and may focus on individual artists, artistic movements, particular works, comparative perspectives, or broader theoretical questions concerning women, gender, and aesthetics. The proposed book seeks to examine the representation, production, and experience of women in art from gendered, cultural, and interdisciplinary perspectives, including but not limited to the following areas: Women artists in historical and contemporary contexts Representations of women in art Women and literature Women in painting, sculpture, and visual arts Women in photography and film Women in theatre, performance, dance, and music Feminist art and feminist aesthetics Gender and artistic representation The female body in art Self-representation and female subjectivity Women, creativity, and authorship Women and artistic institutions Gender inequality and exclusion in the art world Women artists and cultural memory Art, trauma, testimony, and memory Women, war, migration, exile, and displacement Art and resistance Women and political art Women and censorship Queer and intersectional approaches to women and art Race, ethnicity, class, and gender in artistic production Postcolonial and decolonial approaches to women and art Women and indigenous artistic traditions Women and popular culture Digital art, social media, and new forms of female creativity Artificial intelligence, technology, and women in art Women as patrons, collectors, curators, and critics Gendered spaces and artistic production Comparative and interdisciplinary approaches to women and art The book particularly encourages contributions that offer close readings of literary works, films, visual artworks, photography, theatre, performance, music, digital media, or other artistic forms, as well as theoretically grounded analyses that advance current debates on women, gender, and art. We look forward to receiving proposals that critically engage with the intersections of women, creativity, representation, identity, memory, and resistance across artistic and cultural contexts and contribute to ongoing scholarly discussions within Gender Studies, Art Studies, Cultural Studies, Literary Studies, and related fields. Submission Guidelines Abstracts of 200-250 words with 5 keywords. A short biographical note (not more than 150 words), including institutional affiliation and key publications. Please include full contact details. The subject line of the email should state: Submission of Abstracts for the Edited Volume on "Women and Art: Representation, Creativity, and Resistance." Authors selected for inclusion will be invited to submit full chapters (approximately 6,000-7,000 words, including references) following acceptance of the proposal by the publisher. Abstract Submission Deadline: 15 October 2026 Full-Text Submission Deadline: 15 February 2027 Eligibility Contributors are required to hold a PhD. Alternatively, submissions may be co-authored, provided that at least one co-author holds a PhD. In addition, PhD candidates are welcome to submit contributions within their own field of research, particularly if the proposed chapter is directly related to their doctoral project and falls within the thematic and conceptual parameters of this book. Publisher The volume will be published by Maurer Press, Frankfurt am Main, an established publishing house with 35 years of publishing experience. Publication Fee The publication fee for accepted contributions is 115€. Abstracts and inquiries should be sent to: women.art.literature@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: Public Humanities invites submissions for the upcoming themed issue Memorial Culture in Public Art, which will be guest edited by Rebecca Friedman and Alex Lichenstein. The deadline for submissions is October 15, 2026. Description Memorial Culture in Public Art invites submissions that examine the role that art of all kinds - ephemeral public art installations, performances, sculptures, murals, or permanent state-issued monuments - can play in the public's understanding of the past, present, and future. We ask contributors from a multitude of disciplines and from multiple global perspectives to consider how public arts can serve as collective mnemonic inspiration. We invite contributions from academics, public scholars, memory activists, and artists and creatives of all kinds, to explore the role of public art as a form of resistance as it contributes to collective, place-based memory in the face of forces from political ideology and spiritual expression to gentrification and cultural obliteration. Submissions can consist of academic articles, artistic interventions, interviews, dialogues, or other forms. Regardless of format or genre, contributors should engage with questions that include: How have regimes around the globe and across time, whether autocratic or democratic, created-or destroyed--narrative sites of collective memory in public spaces? How can individuals and groups intervene to transform nationalistic, colonial, or dominant narratives through their re-telling and/or transformation of art in public spaces? How can - and have in the past - individuals, groups, communities, neighborhoods, and even nations use(d) art, performance, and display to resist the power of erasure and cultural amnesia? How can public art help usher in a more equitable future based on reconstituting social memory? The current moment witnesses many struggles over memory, as emergent constituencies demand more accountability from public memorial culture while myriad regimes seek to obliterate it. This issue of Public Humanities seeks fresh and innovative approaches across time and spaceto consider these and other conundrums of memory activism and commemorative public art. The editors are especially interested in contributions from and/or about the Global South and the postcolonial world. By engaging the past through its present material and aesthetic manifestations, this issue of Public Humanities will use a host of disciplinary frames to explore how art and commemoration in public spaces open up a window onto how humans navigate space and time through artistic imagination, creativity and expression, and how collective remembering reflects and shapes our contemporary moment. Submission Guidelines Submissions should be written in accessible language for a wide readership across and beyond the humanities; see How to Write for Public Humanities. Articles will be peer reviewed for both content and style. Articles will appear digitally and open access in the journal. All submissions should be made through the Public Humanities online peer review system. Authors should consult the journal's Author Instructions prior to submission. All authors will be required to declare any funding and/or competing interests upon submission. See the journal's Publishing Ethics guidelines for more information. Contacts Dr. Rebecca Friedman | friedmar@fiu.edu Dr. Alex Lichtenstein | alichtens@gmail.com Questions regarding peer review can be sent to the Public Humanities inbox at publichumanities@cambridge.org.

items.fullDescription: "That Sounds Funny": CFP for ALA "Music and the American Literary Imagination" symposium The American Humor Studies Association (AHSA) invites submissions for a proposed panel for the American Literature Association (ALA) 2027 symposium "Music and the American Literary Imagination," to be held January 28-30, 2027, in Nashville, TN. For hundreds of years, humor has been an indelible element of American popular music as well as literature. This AHSA-sponsored, non-guaranteed panel seeks proposals that consider the connections between American humor, American music, and American literature. We invite submissions on any genre, period, or place, including papers that explore the fuzzy boundaries of what it means to be "American." We are especially interested in presentations that examine humor practices in the American South; for example, proposals might consider the use of humor in Southern rap, children's author Shel Silverstein's role in shaping the "outlaw country" sound, or the recent rise of right-wing "humorists" in Nashville. Together, the presentations constituting this panel will explore the pitfalls and possibilities of the imbrication of music, humor, and American literary culture. Please send a 250-word abstract and a brief biography by October 15, 2026, to AHSA Vice President Benjamin Schwartz at bs8959@princeton.edu. All panel participants must be AHSA members before the ALA conference opens on January 28, 2027. The Constance Rourke travel award is available for graduate students on a panel. The award varies between $100 - $300 (depending on AHSA funds and the number of applicants) to help defray the cost of attending conferences with AHSA-sponsored panels. We also remind everyone that AHSA has in place a mentoring program to help emerging scholars prepare an essay for publication. Presenting at ALA can be the first step to being published.

The series editors have already expressed strong in...
items.fullDescription: Edited volume proposed for Manchester University Press's French Film Directors series I am seeking two additional contributors for an edited volume devoted to the work of French filmmaker Nicole Garcia, currently in preparation for submission to Manchester University Press's French Film Directors series. The series editors have already expressed strong interest in the project. Although Garcia has established one of the most distinctive bodies of work in contemporary French cinema-spanning more than three decades and including films such as Place Vendôme (1998), L'Adversaire (2002), Selon Charlie (2006), Un balcon sur la mer (2010), Mal de pierres (2016), and Amants (2020)-her work as a director has received relatively little sustained scholarly attention in either French or English. This volume aims to provide the first comprehensive critical study of Garcia's filmmaking, bringing together scholars from film studies and related disciplines to explore the aesthetic, narrative, thematic, cultural, and institutional dimensions of her work. The project seeks to examine Garcia's cinema through a range of critical and methodological perspectives, combining close analyses of individual films with broader discussions of the contexts in which her work has been produced and received. Contributions informed by interdisciplinary approaches are particularly welcome. Possible areas of inquiry Proposals may address, but are not limited to, the following topics: -Aesthetic and formal strategies: mise-en-scène, spatial construction, narrative ellipsis, secrecy, and revelation. -Genre and narrative form: melodrama, romantic narratives, psychological drama, and narrative complexity. -Adaptation and screenwriting: literary adaptation, intermediality, and processes of cinematic creation. -Gender and subjectivity: female desire, intimacy, ambivalence, vulnerability, and representations of femininity. -Performance and authorship: Garcia's trajectory from actress to filmmaker, her direction of actors, and her engagement with stardom. -Social relations and identities: masculinity, class, family relationships, and bourgeois social worlds. -Memory and temporality: nostalgia, personal and collective memory, displacement, and the relationship between past and present. -Industrial and institutional contexts: production and funding structures, festival circulation, and the position of women directors within the French film industry. -Comparative and interdisciplinary approaches: connections with other filmmakers, European art cinema, literature, gender studies, memory studies, cultural studies, and related fields. Contributors are welcome to focus on one or more individual films, provided their analyses engage with the broader concerns of the volume. Comparative approaches are also encouraged, with Garcia's directorial work remaining central to the discussion. The volume seeks not only to foreground Garcia's contribution as a filmmaker but also to use her work as a lens through which to explore broader questions of authorship, gender, cinematic form, and the cultural economy of contemporary French cinema. Submission guidelines The volume is expected to comprise approximately 10-12 chapters of 6,000-7,000 words each. Prospective contributors are invited to submit an abstract of approximately 500 words, clearly outlining the proposed chapter's central argument, theoretical or methodological framework, and the specific aspects of Garcia's cinema it will examine. Submissions should also include: -Full name and current institutional affiliation; -Contact information; -A short biographical note. Deadline for abstracts: October 15, 2026 Please submit your proposal using the following link: https://www.dropbox.com/request/ykp0stxbqk5dhsjnhl7m The book proposal is scheduled for submission to Manchester University Press in fall 2026. The deadline for completed chapters will be communicated once the publication timetable has been established, and contributors will be given sufficient time to prepare their manuscripts. Scholars at all career stages, including early-career researchers, are warmly encouraged to submit proposals. Editor and contact Dr Romain Chareyron (roc104@usask.ca) Associate Professor of French Department of Languages, Literatures and Cultural Studies University of Saskatchewan, Canada

items.title: Eating for a Green Future : Literature, Culture, and the Politics of Food in Contemporary India
items.excerpt: CALL FOR CHAPTER PROPOSALS Eating for a Green Future: Literature, Culture, and the Politics of Food in Contemporary India Edited by Dr. Manisha Mohanty (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University & Fulbright-Nehru Fellow) Dr. Shashibhusan Nayak (MLA Bibliography Fellow, MLA) Dr. Sonali Das (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University) This edited volume begins from...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTER PROPOSALS Eating for a Green Future: Literature, Culture, and the Politics of Food in Contemporary India Edited by Dr. Manisha Mohanty (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University & Fulbright-Nehru Fellow) Dr. Shashibhusan Nayak (MLA Bibliography Fellow, MLA) Dr. Sonali Das (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University) This edited volume begins from a single premise: food cannot be discussed apart from the politics that surround it. Questions around production and consumption are inseparable from issues of hunger, malnutrition, social inequality, and ecological crisis. The concept of 'food culture', understood as the cooking and eating of food, must be reexamined in the light of sustainability and structural violence. Industrial agriculture, multinational food corporations, and extreme disparities in access have made eating an exercise of power as much as of nourishment. In India, the evidence is stark. Farmer suicides, shrinking biodiversity, corporate-controlled food systems, and climate-induced crop failures expose the systemic inequalities that run through the country's foodways. The volume gathers essays on literature, film, digital media, and everyday food practice, investigating how contemporary texts address climate change, agribusiness, land dispossession, toxic labour, and food scarcity. One question threads through the whole collection: how much of what we eat still comes from traditional, community-based knowledge, and how much is determined by global agribusiness, whose interest lies in maximizing profit rather than social welfare or universal nourishment? This leads us to explore how corporate food systems blur the distinction between inherited culinary practices and their commodified imitations. The result is a food culture in which authenticity itself becomes a marketing strategy. This volume works across food studies, environmental humanities, and popular culture, and its ambition is both practical and critical: to propose justice-oriented frameworks for rethinking consumption, appetite, and sustainability. Proposed Themes: • Food and sustainability: How can food culture foreground sustainability and ecological concerns rather than mere novelty or elitist pleasure? • Culinary knowledge and agribusiness: How much of what we eat today emerges from traditional ecological knowledge, local seed cultures, and community foodways, and what is shaped by agribusiness, multinational food corporations, and algorithmically curated "choices"? • Rethinking consumption: How can we rethink everyday modes of eating, cooking, and appetite to bring about positive ecological change and more equitable food systems? • Power and intersectionality: How does the intersection of food studies and environmental studies illuminate caste, class, and racial hierarchies, gendered labour, and entrenched social inequalities? • Food justice: How do literary texts, films, digital campaigns, and social media food cultures imagine or fail to imagine food justice, and how might these imaginaries inform public policy and activism? Proposed Structure: Part I: Food, Ecology, and Justice · Food politics, food justice, and environmental humanities · Traditional ecological knowledge and culinary/cultural memory · Rethinking appetite and taste in times of climate crisis Part II: Literature, Film, and Visual Culture · Novels and memoirs centred on famine, scarcity, or ecological degradation · Regional food literatures · Films that foreground drought, crop failure, farmer suicides, or agrarian distress Part III: Digital Foodscapes, Social Media, Influencers, and Algorithms · Hashtag activism around hunger, food waste, land rights, and seed sovereignty · Corporate influence in online food marketing · Online recipe cultures as spaces of resistance (low-waste cooking, foraging, veganism, zero-waste influencers, etc.) Part IV: Politics and the Future of Food · Analysing policy texts, food security laws, and welfare schemes through a cultural lens · Grassroots food sovereignty movements, community kitchens, seed banks · Frameworks for sustainable and just food futures grounded in local knowledge systems · Pedagogy: teaching food-environment issues in classrooms, community settings, and online spaces Part V: Special Section India/Odisha · Indigenous and Adivasi food knowledge · Cyclone-prone ecologies and coastal food insecurity · Temple food cultures · Gendered kitchen labour in rural and urban India/Odisha · Caste-based food taboos and community food practices · Land, mining, and displacement affecting food systems Submission Guidelines: We invite scholars, independent researchers, and practitioners working in literary and cultural studies, environmental humanities, food studies, media studies, and related fields to submit original, unpublished chapter proposals. Interdisciplinary and comparative approaches are especially encouraged. Proposals should include: • An abstract of 300-350 words outlining the chapter's argument, methodology, and primary texts or case studies • 5-6 keywords • A short biographical note (75-100 words) with full name, institutional affiliation, and contact details Full chapters should be: • 5,000-8,000 words in length, inclusive of notes and references • Follow MLA style (9th edition) • Original, previously unpublished, and not under review elsewhere Timeline: • Abstract submission deadline: 15 October 2026 • Notification of acceptance: 20 November 2026 • Full chapter submission: 28 February 2027 Submission: Please send abstracts and biographical notes as a single Word document to: Dr. Shashibhusan Nayak: shashienglish@gmail.com and Dr. Manisha Mohanty: manishamohanty@soa.ac.in Publication: Following the review of abstracts and full chapters, the completed manuscript will be submitted to Bloomsbury for consideration. All chapters will undergo peer review as part of the standard editorial and publisher review process.

items.fullDescription: European Comic Art Special Issue 'Francophone Graphic Narratives / Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance' European Comic Art invites proposals for a special issue on 'Francophone Graphic Narratives/Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance'. This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its many forms - political, cultural, institutional, and aesthetic - and how they forge practices of resistance and dissent. The bande dessinée is a medium that subverts hierarchies and blurs boundaries. Long regarded as the lowly offspring of literature and the visual arts, comics have since been legitimised by scholars and artists demonstrating their capacity to engage with complex sociohistorical, political, and cultural topics. This 'Ninth Art' now occupies an increasingly important place in university classrooms, academic publications, and public discourse alike. Its multimodal features - panel layout, gutters, framing, braiding, and complex interplay between text and image - allow comics to stage and challenge authority in formally distinctive ways. This aesthetic vantage point makes comics a powerful medium through which to bring displaced, excluded, and silenced narratives into view. From Chantal Montellier's impressive four-decade oeuvre of political cartoons and graphic novels contesting racism, misogyny and totalitarianism to Jessica Oublié's Peyi an nou , which provides a counternarrative to state discourse on the BUMIDOM, the bande dessinée has often served to undercut official rhetoric. This special issue of European Comic Art seeks articles that examine how Francophone bandes dessinées engage with dominant institutions and discourses from theoretical and pedagogical perspectives. How do comics represent power and powerlessness? How do they respond to hierarchies that exist in various settings and communities? How do they decentre and challenge 'standard' language practices? Finally, how might comics be used pedagogically to help foster students' critical thinking skills and question institutional, political, and social discourses? Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Migration Ecocriticism Social justice and political activism Gender and sexuality Comics and memory studies Class, labour, and economic inequality Pedagogy and second language acquisition Nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and globalization Colonial legacies, decolonial resistance/critique Monolingualism, multilingualism, and language politics Official histories, counter archives, and silenced narratives Humour, parody, satire, and subversion Submission Guidelines Please submit a 500-word abstract with a short biographical note to Liana Pshevorska at lpshevorska@wesleyan.edu and Valentina Denzel at vdenzel@msu.edu by October 15, 2026. Informal inquiries are welcome. Decisions will be communicated in November 2026. The deadline for submitting full manuscripts is February 28, 2027. Articles should be in English, approximately 8,000 words, including images, notes, and bibliography. Contributors may include up to four images, which will be factored into the overall length of the article. Each image will be counted as approximately three-quarters of a printed page, based on an estimate 400 words per page. Please note that authors are responsible for obtaining copyright permission for all included images. Documentation of permissions should be submitted alongside the manuscript.

items.fullDescription: Art and the Making of Belonging: Migration, Mobility & Communities in Formation March 19-20, 2027 State Historical Society of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri How do people create a sense of home and belonging in places shaped by migration and mobility? How do communities sustain traditions, negotiate change, and build connections across difference? In confronting these pressing issues of our time, art and culture often play a central role, serving as powerful tools in building relationships, negotiating difference, and making space for new forms of collective life. The Interdisciplinary Migration Studies Institute invites artists, activists, performers, faith leaders, educators, community organizers, cultural workers, students, migrants, and scholars to join us for a community event that explores this relationship between migration, mobility, creativity, and community. We welcome participants from all backgrounds and encourage contributions that draw on lived experience, creative practice, community engagement, research, or combinations of these approaches. We especially welcome participants who can share their knowledge and experience about the following questions: · How have artistic collaborations created spaces where people from different cultural, linguistic, or religious backgrounds can encounter one another in new ways? · How have communities used art to navigate difference, address tensions, and build connections across lines of migration, identity, and experience? · What role does participation in artistic and cultural life play in fostering belonging for both newcomers and established community members? · How have artists, organizers, educators, faith leaders, and community groups used creative practices to cultivate trust, solidarity, and a shared sense of belonging? · How have museums, cultural institutions, libraries, religious institutions, schools, public spaces, and community organizations used the arts to support meaningful encounters between immigrants and longer-standing community members? The event will feature short presentations, roundtable discussions, performances, workshops, and a gallery exhibition at the State Historical Society of Missouri showcasing projects and creative works. We encourage submissions from individuals and groups. Proposals may be submitted as individual presentations, performances, workshops, exhibits, panels, or other formats that support engagement and dialogue. If you have an idea that does not fit neatly into a traditional conference format, we would be delighted to hear from you. Participation Formats Presentations Presentations will typically be organized into thematic panels consisting of three 20-minute presentations followed by discussion. Presenters will have access to audiovisual support for slide presentations. Roundtable Discussions Roundtables bring together a small group of participants to engage in moderated conversation and audience discussion. Rather than formal presentations, roundtables emphasize dialogue, shared experiences, and collective reflection. We welcome proposals for complete roundtables as well as individual expressions of interest. Workshops Workshops are one-hour, hands-on sessions designed to teach attendees (up to 25 participants) a particular creative practice, collaborative method, or community-engagement approach. Audiovisual support will be available. Media and Performance We welcome both live and recorded performances that showcase or model artistic collaboration. Our venue can accommodate musical, dance, theatrical, spoken-word, and multimedia performances, as well as filmed versions of these forms. Gallery Exhibition The event will feature an accompanying exhibition showcasing artistic, cultural, educational, and community-based projects related to migration, belonging, and community formation. Projects may include visual art, photography, documentary work, storytelling initiatives, community-engaged arts projects, digital media, educational exhibits, oral history projects, and other creative or collaborative endeavors. Proposal Submission Guidelines All proposals must be submitted through the online application portal. The following information is required for all submission types: · Title of the proposed presentation, workshop, performance, or project · Name(s) of all participant(s) · Email address(es) of all participant(s) In addition, please submit the materials listed below for your selected participation format. Panel Presentations · A description of the proposed presentation (300 words or fewer) · A brief biographical statement, including institutional affiliation if applicable (50 words or fewer) Roundtable Discussions · A description of the experience, perspective, or expertise you would bring to the discussion (300 words or fewer) · A brief biographical statement, including institutional affiliation if applicable (50 words or fewer) Workshops · A description of the proposed workshop and its goals (300 words or fewer) · A brief biographical statement, including institutional affiliation if applicable, and relevant experience leading workshops (100 words or fewer) Media and Performance · A description of the proposed performance and its relationship to the event theme (300 words or fewer) · Length of the performance · A description of any on-site needs, including audiovisual equipment, changing rooms, or other accommodations Gallery Exhibition · A project description that includes a statement explaining the project's relevance to the event theme (300 words or fewer) · Up to five images, links, or other supporting materials · A description of display and technical requirements, including needs for wall space, table space, digital displays, audio equipment, or other resources Deadline for Submissions: October 15, 2026 Submit Proposals here: https://missouri.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_4Inv3NNBs7ov7P8

items.title: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities
items.excerpt: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative a...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. We encourage essays focused on narratives as well as submissions that explore art installations and other medial forms that address the boundary waters circulating around and through the blue humanities. Topics may include but are not limited to the following: Boundary waters that divide and connect nations, classes, and/or ecological zones Mythic, cinematic, and visual narratives of how humans and/or nonhumans are "held," migrate, or are moved through watery littorals Critical explorations like those associated with "tidalectics," a term that comes from Kamau Brathwaite, who proposed an alternative framework for literary and political engagement that is grounded in the rhythm of waves and the cyclic ebb and flow of tides "Portraits" of littoral space(s) in literature, history, myth, the visual arts, and theatrical and musical performances Exploring the significance of physical, structural, and emotional vulnerabilities and instabilities within littorals, shoals, or port cities Hydrological infrastructure (colonial, postcolonial, urban, rural) associated with port cities, canal locks, and dams Relational undercurrents that speak to our ways of submerging ourselves into the watery worlds that surround us Traditional water ways: ways of being with or "holding" water The role of inland waterways in routing stories and/or facilitating/impeding human and nonhuman migrations Exploring the agency of oceans and rivers in sustaining capitalist and imperial economies and their alternatives Water's many forms (snow, ice, fog, rivers, oceans) and ways "water" facilitates connection and/or imposes isolation How waterways-"paths" of water and ways of being with water-lead us to new or alternative futures Scenes of erosion that expose lost or forgotten histories Please direct questions to the special issue editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri [edkunkur@mtu.edu] and Dana Van Kooy [drvankoo@mtu.edu] For questions about the use and disclosure of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, please see NANO's AI Statement (https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Journal-Information) Please use the Submission Form on top left of the CFP page: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Submissions/Submission-Form NANO: New American Notes Online is a free, open-access, peer-reviewed journal. NANO does not charge for submission, review, or publication. It is indexed in the MLA International Bibliography, GALE, ProQuest, and DOAJ.

items.fullDescription: The erotic is a point of infinite signification, a navel in humanity’s symbolic circuit. However, despite its resistance to formalization, it is always in the process of not being written. As Octavio Paz insists, the erotic is a metaphor indelible to the human. As such, it is unsurprising that the manifestations of the erotic in subjective embodied experience are variable and correspond to equally plural treatments of it across the academic panorama. This diverse archive is bound by certain distinguishable threads, in terms of the potentiality of the erotic, its singular relation to language, and to the sphere of sexuality.

items.excerpt: Conference Theme: Beyond Repair: Reconciliations, Restorations, Resurgences Conference Dates: February 10-12, 2027 Submission Deadline: October 23, 2026 The African, African American, and Diaspora Studies Center at James Madison University invites proposals for its annual interdisciplinary conference Beyond Repair: Reconciliations, Restorations, Resurgenc...
items.fullDescription: Conference Theme: Beyond Repair: Reconciliations, Restorations, Resurgences Conference Dates: February 10-12, 2027 Submission Deadline: October 23, 2026 The African, African American, and Diaspora Studies Center at James Madison University invites proposals for its annual interdisciplinary conference Beyond Repair: Reconciliations, Restorations, Resurgences. The conference will be held from Wednesday, February 10 to Friday, February 12, 2027 and brings together scholars, archivists, and practitioners from a variety of overlapping and intersecting fields. Submit proposals by October 23, 2026. Repair has become one of the defining political and ethical vocabularies of our moment. Calls for reparations have generated new ways of imagining justice, accountability, and redress, while also raising questions about whether the language of repair is itself sufficient to address the enduring legacies of colonialism and slavery. This year's theme "Beyond Repair" gestures simultaneously in two directions: it evokes what may appear irreparable, but it also invites debate over what we mean by "repair" in the first place. What can it achieve? What are its limits? What lies past its horizons? What in our present condition is beyond repair, and where does this leave us for imagining a future that does justice to the past? This year's conference will be hybrid; we invite in-person and virtual presentations on all topics relevant to AAAD studies, even if not directly pertinent to the conference theme. We welcome proposals from scholars from all disciplines at any point in their scholarly careers. Proposals for individual presentations or pre-constituted panels could address, but are not limited to, topics such as the following: · Reparations and reparative structures · Post-conflict recovery · Frameworks of restorative justice · Relief and its discontents · Reconciliation and refusal · Resurgence and renewal · Community restoration · Global and transnational partnerships · Historical reckoning · Memory and forgetting · Archives and recovery · Narrative repair · Healing and health · Arts of restoration · Religious communities and social repair · Ecological restoration · Climate resilience · Land and belonging · Diasporic networks · Pedagogies of repair · Reproductive justice · Literary resurgences · Queer histories and futures · Transitional justice · Care and community · Reparative economy · Wealth and debt · Digital storytelling Please submit either a 300-word individual paper proposal or 1000-word panel proposal on the appropriate form linked below by October 23, 2026. Panel proposals must include at least three panelists. For panels, acceptance information will be sent directly to the panel organizer. Individual Paper Submission Form: https://forms.gle/rB6N9EB1MKNZAxBBA Panel Submission Form: https://forms.gle/5rCwccWXPFfxcgGw9 Further information and updates about the conference may be found at sites.lib.jmu.edu/aaadjmu. International respondents traveling to the United States in need of Visa documentation are encouraged to submit their abstracts as early as possible, ideally before September 15. International respondents will be notified on an ongoing basis after submitting their proposal. US respondents will be notified within a month after the deadline. Questions may be sent to aaadstudies@jmu.edu.

items.location: University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) · Penn Graduate Jewish Studies
items.excerpt: Jewish Life between Locality and Mobility Penn Graduate Conference in Jewish Studies, February 28-March 1, 2027 Throughout many periods of their histories, Jews and Jewish communities have developed an ambivalent relationship to the spaces in which they have lived. Jewish collective memory is deeply rooted in the land of Israel, both real and imagined, wh...
items.fullDescription: Jewish Life between Locality and Mobility Penn Graduate Conference in Jewish Studies, February 28-March 1, 2027 Throughout many periods of their histories, Jews and Jewish communities have developed an ambivalent relationship to the spaces in which they have lived. Jewish collective memory is deeply rooted in the land of Israel, both real and imagined, while simultaneously grounded in a wide array of diasporic localities. From "the wandering Jew" and "the rootless cosmopolitan" to the image of the assimilated Jew, conceptions of Jewishness have been shaped by the contested but strong, ever-evolving ties Jews had to the spaces they inhabited. In modern times, as the Jewish national movement took shape and eventually led to the establishment of the State of Israel, Jews around the world continue to grapple with questions of identity and belonging, safety, resilience, and autonomy in a world where Jewish sovereignty exists alongside longstanding Jewish communities in the diaspora. The Jewish Studies Graduate Conference at the University of Pennsylvania, to be held on the Penn campus in Philadelphia on February 28-March 1, 2027, seeks to explore the relationship between locality and mobility in Jewish life across historical periods and geographical spaces. This interdisciplinary conference will serve as a forum for graduate students to share their research, receive feedback from Penn faculty and fellow graduate students, and learn about ongoing work in the field from peers around the world. We aim to foster a community of emerging scholars who will help shape the global future of Jewish Studies. We welcome contributions from the wide array of disciplines connected with Jewish Studies, including but not limited to: Ancient History Anthropology Archaeology Architecture Art History Geography History Jewish Languages (Hebrew, Ladino, Yiddish, etc.) Linguistics Literary Studies Media Studies Museum Studies Religious Studies Travel and accommodation: Thanks to the generous support of our sponsors, we are able to provide presenters with up to two nights of accommodation in Philadelphia. Limited funds are also available for presenters from outside the Philadelphia area to help defray the cost of travel (economy fare) to and from the conference. To apply: Submit your abstract, not to exceed 300 words, via this link: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdWszlWuD3IeBHGzQgikSNqOTvTaIfZpEI5kcv988WIw6JVlg/viewform?usp=header by October 30. items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. Indexing Information for Prospective Authors IGI Global Scientific Publishing meets the criteria for inclusion in major indexing services such as Scopus; however, it is important to note that all indexing decisions are made independently by these services. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. items.fullDescription: Folklore is having a moment in South Asian writing, and it isn't a nostalgic one. items.fullDescription: What is the real difference between speaking with nature and speaking for it? Is eco-centric thought a universally shared ideology, or does it develop in reaction to historical, philosophical, and socio-cultural contexts? In what way do the fundamental principles of Indian ecology vary from prevailing Western structures? These essential inquiries delineate the parameters of Ramachandra Guha’s Speaking with Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism (2024), which effectively contests the notion that environmentalism is a unidirectional phenomenon dictated by Western influence. This view posits that the rest of the world, particularly the Global South, lacks eco-conscious awareness because it is ‘too poor to be green’.

items.fullDescription: In India, the displacement of Adivasis, tribals, poor, farmers, forest-dwelling and land-based people, and other marginalized communities for development and infrastructure projects like dams, railways, power projects, and bridge construction, or for capitalist accumulation like mining, resource extraction, tourism, and industry, is a common occurrence. Although such projects are implemented for the sake of the ‘greater common good’ for all, only a few elites enjoy the benefit of these projects, depriving millions of displaced, marginalized people (Roy 1999).

One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. The Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies area invites paper proposals on topics related to Taylor Swift and/or Swifties from multiple vantage points. Since her debut in 2006, Taylor Swift has become a fixture of popular culture. Her career has been marked by incredible record-breaking highs and infamous tabloid-fodder lows. Known for her sharp lyrics, her evolving cross-genre musical styles, and her dedicated, creative fanbase (the Swifties), Swift's influence has been noted within music, fashion, economics, politics, and other cultural spheres of power. As an interdisciplinary area, we invite papers from multiple perspectives and disciplines. Topics might include, but are not limited to: • Critical interpretations of Swift's lyrics, eras, and/or personas • Considerations of Taylor Swift and politics, feminisms, activism and social justice • Interrogations of Swift and gender, race, class, and other identities/identifications • Analyses of Swift's connections to business, law, psychology, philosophy or other academic disciplines • Arguments about fandom, belonging, relating, creating and other Swiftie concerns • Examples of Taylor Swift's pedagogical relevancy All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. SWPACA offers monetary awards for the best graduate student papers in a variety of categories. Submissions of accepted, full papers are due January 1, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Taylor Swift and Swiftie Studies area, please contact its Area Chair, Juliette Holder at jholder1@csustan.edu. If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic invites proposals relating to magical worldviews, practices, and representations, as well as consciousness transformation, the preternatural, the paranormal, hidden meanings, the power of transmutation, and related phenomena. Characteristic methods, beliefs, perspectives, paradigms and techniques include: arcane symbolism, imagery, and aesthetics; unseen forces, spiritual intermediaries, invisible agencies, nonhuman intelligences; synchronous patterns, non-ordinary causation, and anomalous processes. Examples of ideas and systems include Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Sufism, Tantra, Rosicrucianism, Freemasonry, Satanism, witchcraft, sorcery, demonology, astrology, alchemy, yoga, shamanism, parapsychology, as well as psychic and paranormal phenomena, along with beliefs and practices relating to altered states of consciousness, overlapping with the study of mysticism and New Age spirituality, channeling, positive thinking, manifestation, reality shifting, the power of intention, numerology, guardian angels, and Ascended Masters. Esoteric, occult, and magical concepts, beliefs, and practices appear in every culture and civilization; contemporary media and popular culture have embraced them enthusiastically, yet at times have reacted against them. The impact of esotericism, occultism, and magic on genre formation/content and popular cultural perceptions has been profound.
