items.title: The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature
items.excerpt: CALL FOR CHAPTERS The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature Editors: Mariusz Finkielsztein (University of Gdan?sk) mariusz.finkielsztein@gmail.com Josefa Ros Velasco (Complutense University of Madrid) josros@ucm.es The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature is to be a comprehensive monographic study examining boredom as a central aesthetic, philosoph...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTERS The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature Editors: Mariusz Finkielsztein (University of Gdan?sk) mariusz.finkielsztein@gmail.com Josefa Ros Velasco (Complutense University of Madrid) josros@ucm.es The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature is to be a comprehensive monographic study examining boredom as a central aesthetic, philosophical, psychological, and socio-cultural category in the history of modern literature. Rather than relying purely on abstract theory, this volume approaches boredom through focused case studies devoted to individual authors and their works. Across these chapters, boredom-alongside adjacent states such as ennui, tedium, spleen, acedia, melancholy, existential malaise, and affective exhaustion-emerges variously as paralysis, protest, privilege, illness, and spiritual crisis. By situating close textual readings within the broader intellectual history of modernity, the volume, written by a multidisciplinary group of authors, is to demonstrate that literary boredom is a powerful diagnostic lens on social order, temporality, and the modern subject's experience of meaninglessness. Volume Structure & Epochal Scope The volume is planned as a Handbook or Companion and covers not only the most vital writers addressing the theme of boredom but also a broad selection of modern authors (around 60 chapters). The book is to trace the evolution of literary boredom across (tentatively) seven historical and thematic phases: Early Modernity & Enlightenment Foundations: Early reflections on existential void and social routine (e.g. Diderot, Laclos, Austen). Romantic Ennui (1770s-1840s): Melancholy, idealist frustration, and the world-weary anti-hero (e.g., Goethe, de Stae?l, Senancour, Byron, Chateaubriand, Constant, Stendhal, Sand, Balzac, Musset). The Superfluous Man: The Russian literary archetype of social paralysis, alienation, and unfulfilled potential (e.g. Pushkin, Lermontov, Goncharov, Turgenev). Bourgeois Boredom, Realism, & Decadent Spleen: Domestic stagnation, industrial monotony, social entrapment, and aesthetic decay (e.g., Dickens, Flaubert, Tolstoy, Fontane, Chopin, Ibsen, Gilman, Conrad, Chekhov, Baudelaire, Huysmans, Wilde). Modernist Stagnation (Early 20th C.): Temporal distortion, consciousness, alienation, and metaphysical paralysis (e.g., Proust, Joyce, Pessoa, Mann, Kafka, Woolf). Catastrophism & Existential Absurdity (Mid-20th C.): Totalitarian dread, the absurdity of existence, and postwar existential malaise (e.g., Broch, Platonov, Orwell, H. Miller, Gombrowicz, Sartre, Camus, Beckett, Buzzati, Gracq). Postwar Emptiness, Consumerism, & Digital Fatigue: Mass society, late-capitalist hyper-consumption, information overload, and contemporary affective exhaustion (e.g., Moravia, Perec, de Beauvoir, Ernaux, Bellow, Bernhard, Duras, DeLillo, Houellebecq, Ferrante, Rourke, Moshfegh). Chapter Guidelines & Scope Each chapter must offer an in-depth analysis of the theme of broadly understood boredom in the work of a single author (according to a formula: Boredom in...). The title should include the name and surname of a writer as a main part, and a freely formulated subtitle. Analytical Approach: Authors may focus on a single representative work but should analyse boredom across multiple texts of an author to demonstrate how boredom functions as a recurring motif in the author's oeuvre. Target Audience: Written primarily for readers seeking to deepen their understanding of boredom in a specific author's work (spoilers are permitted), while remaining accessible to a general literary audience. Comparative analysis with other writers should be kept to a minimum. Required Contextual Elements: o Biographical Context: Key details situating the writer within their epoch. Where applicable, personal engagement with boredom (e.g., excerpts from letters, diaries) may be included. o Socio-Cultural Context: Historical background necessary to understand the specific societal structures depicting boredom (e.g., aristocratic class dynamics, marital systems, late-capitalist work environments, author's country history and socio-cultural context). Submission guidelines: The abstract of the proposed chapter (between 250-500 words) along with a short bio (up to 150 words) and contact information should be sent to editors via e-mail before the end of October 2026. Contributors may propose up to two chapters. Each submission must include a brief statement detailing: (a) how the chosen author's work relates to boredom; and (b) what the contributor's expertise is on the writer. The minimum criteria for inclusion of a writer are: the author must address themes of boredom/ennui, possess at least some international recognition, and be available in English translation. Poetry is excluded. The comments and decisions on the proposed chapters will be provided before the end of December 2026. Then, the proposal for the book will be sent to prospective publishers (Routledge Handbook Series, The Oxford Handbooks, The Cambridge Companions or The Palgrave Handbooks). In case of a positive answer from a publisher, the authors will be asked to prepare the chapter, between 6,000 and 8,000 words including footnotes and references. Technical information will be provided after the publisher accepts the proposal and will depend on the publisher's style. In case of any doubts and/or questions, we encourage prospective authors to consult the editors directly. Prospective deadline for chapters: mid-2028

items.fullDescription: John Steinbeck once remarked that fellow-Californian Robinson Jeffers wrote some the "greatest poetry since Whitman." Steinbeck kept a significant collection of Jeffers work both in his personal library and Ed Ricketts' Lab, where Jeffers was an influential topic in their endlessly varied conversations. When asked about possibility of meeting the poet, Steinbeck declined with a telling degree of reverence: "His poetry is perfect to me, and I don't think one should get the man mixed up with his work." Although they did eventually meet-notably when Steinbeck lived in Monterey in 1944-their relationship was one of distant, though friendly, mutual respect. Although these two writers rarely crossed physical paths, their work maintains a wide concurrence of concern. They both deeply engaged with Californian geography and history; they both emphasized the influence of the natural world upon the individual and society; they both had social circles that revolved around the Monterey Peninsula; they both were interested in psychoanalytical theory; they both were students of classical literature and philosophy; they both experienced extraordinary recognition at the peak of their literary fame (at one point, Jeffers was on the cover of Time magazine); they both were deeply uncomfortable with such a cultural spotlight; they both admonished personal humility in the face of environmental forces. Intersections such as these (and many more) deserve to be explored with more depth and significance. The editorial staff at the Steinbeck Review invites submissions for a special edition, "John Steinbeck and Robinson Jeffers." We are particularly interested in perspectives which put these authors into conversation in productive and even unexpected ways. Although submissions are not required to examine both authors, we strongly suggest that they engage (even if briefly) both Steinbeck and Jeffers. We welcome all critical and theoretical perspectives. Please see the full guide for submissions here and submit your paper to the Steinbeck Review's online submission system, found at www.editorialmanager.com/Steinbeck, no later than October 31, 2026. Decisions will be made by December 1, 2026. Submissions should be accompanied by an abstract and key words.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Siren! Magazine Second Issue: Disciplined Bodies, Transgressive Bodies, Transformed Bodies Link to the call: https://penn.manifoldapp.org/page/siren-current-call-for-proposals Bodies are shaped by the worlds we inhabit, the stories we tell about them, and the institutions through which we learn what a body is, what it should look like, how it should behave, and what it is permitted to become. Yet bodies are often treated as merely biological facts: fixed, self-evident, and prior to politics. This distinction matters because once something is understood as natural, the expectations attached to it can begin to appear inevitable. For this issue, we invite work on disciplined, transgressive, and transformed bodies. We are interested in work that reflects on how bodily norms are produced and enforced, what happens when bodies exceed or destabilize those norms, and how bodies are remade through political, social, technological, medical, aesthetic, and cultural processes. The question, then, is not only who tells bodies what to do, but how we come to understand what bodies are for in the first place and how we may challenge the constraints imposed over them. How do medicine, law, media, family, religion, workplaces, markets, states, and digital platforms make particular kinds of bodies appear normal, desirable, healthy, productive, legible, or valuable? What happens when a body does not fit the meaning assigned to it; when it refuses, cannot comply, fails to conform, or becomes something else? We are especially interested in moments when bodily categories begin to break down, when the meanings attached to bodies no longer hold, or become further reinforced and are resisted, and when bodies become sites of contradiction, refusal, negotiation, and possibility. Key terms For the purposes of this issue, we understand the three terms broadly and provisionally: Disciplined bodies are shaped by the norms, institutions, and expectations that surround them. They may be expected to reproduce, perform gender recognizably, be deemed healthy and desirable, remain productive and self-optimizing, regulate themselves, and stay intelligible to others. We welcome work on how these norms are produced, enforced, negotiated, and unevenly distributed. Transgressive bodies make those expectations difficult to sustain. Transgression need not be intentional: a body may refuse, fail, exceed, disrupt, or simply be unable to comply. Nor are particular bodies inherently transgressive; they are often rendered so by institutions and cultural frameworks that mark some forms of embodiment as abnormal, excessive, threatening, or unintelligible. Transformed bodies ask what happens when embodiments become a site of remaking. Bodies may be altered through medicine, technology, disability, transition, reproduction, labor, aging, artistic practice, environmental exposure, or political violence. Transformation may be desired or imposed, liberatory, or coercive. We are interested in what bodies become, what histories they carry, what forms of power shape them, and what futures they make imaginable. We welcome submissions that interpret one of these categories, bring two or more into conversation, question the distinctions between them, or propose other ways of thinking about bodily discipline, transgression, and transformation. Proposals should identify the term that most strongly connects to the submission while noting any significant intersections with the others. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: -Bodily autonomy and reproductive rights -Disability and debility -Gender and sexuality -Race and racialization -Beauty and aesthetic labor -Health, illness, and wellness -Medicine and biomedical technologies -Aging -Death -War and militarization -Sport and physical performance -Embodiment and mediation (digital or otherwise) -Surveillance -Cyborg subjectivities -Body modification -Bodily aesthetics -Migration and borders -Carcerality -Labor and productivity -Environmental harm -Colonialism and its afterlives -Speculative or imagined forms of embodiment Who can submit We welcome work from scholars, students, artists, activists, independent researchers, and public intellectuals working in communication, media studies, feminist studies, cultural studies, disability studies, queer and trans studies, critical race studies, the humanities, and related fields. Submissions are open to contributors at all career stages, but we particularly encourage work from early-career scholars and those whose work may sit outside conventional academic publishing structures. Formats Submissions may be written, visual, audiovisual, audio, or hybrid. We welcome experimental forms alongside conventional scholarly approaches. Across formats, submissions should engage the issue's broader commitments to critical feminist inquiry, transnational solidarity, feminist world-making, and transformative social change. Timeline For full consideration, abstracts are due by October 31, 2026, with decisions made by December 10th. Completed submissions will be due by February 10th, 2027, with a projected publication date in September 2027. Guidelines for proposal types -Paper: Please send the title and a 250-word abstract outlining the argument for a full paper featuring an original contribution. Full papers are long-form (3000-5000 words) analytical essays that connect to the current topic of the issue. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Escalator Paper: Please submit the title and a 150-word abstract for a short analytical piece (500-2000 words). Research escalator papers are works-in-progress on novel ideas related to the issue theme; they will be published as submitted and paired with an expert mentor to develop into a full analytical or empirical work. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Multimedia and Hybrid Submissions: Please submit the title and a 200-250-word description explaining how your piece relates to the current issue's theme. For multimedia works, explain how text and other elements interact. Finished pieces should include a link to a sample. For works in progress, add a brief (up to 100 words) outline of the concept, your process, and the timeline for completion. Experimental submissions are encouraged. Important dates Abstract due: October 31, 2026 Acceptances: December 10, 2026 Final submission: February 10, 2027 Peer-review process and mentorships: February - June 2027 Expected publication date: early September 2027 All proposals should be sent as a .docx or .pdf document, and include a brief bio (up to 150 words) introducing yourself and your background. Please submit proposals to asc-sirenmagazine@asc.upenn.edu, using the subject line "Siren Magazine - Bodies." Direct any questions regarding the call or submission process to the same address.

Call for papers | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power "We are mythmaking creatures" (Ware 20...
items.fullDescription: Call for papers | Diffractions Issue 13 | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power? Deadline for Abstracts: October 31st 2026 Deadline for Papers: January 31st 2027 Editors-in-Chief: Alyse Kaweng Fan, Thales Reis Alecrim? Call for papers | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power "We are mythmaking creatures" (Ware 2025); human beings make and reinterpret myths. Mythmaking has remained a living action of the human cultural process since the earliest stage of human history. Myths are not static stories that stay unchanged across time; that is why agency and acts of mythmaking are powerful. Through mythmaking, inherited stories are continually adapted and reinterpreted to reflect changing cultural values and historical circumstances. Consequently, myth also assumes the form of a spectacle and ideology that must be critically examined; it often serves to naturalise or essentialise instances of domination, transforming contingent political agendas into "universal" truths. This call for papers values both the aesthetic brilliance of mythmaking in the arts and popular culture and the rigor critique of its ideological utility as a tool for hegemony. The inherent ambiguity of myth as both a meaning-making tool and a mechanism of control invites further scholarly exploration. We therefore seek to gather diverse perspectives on how these creative processes function across human experience, inviting interdisciplinary submissions that weave together multifaceted theories of myth and mythmaking.?? Even the same myth can be retold in radically different ways. For Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, the reinvented myth of Ozymandias represents a meditation on antiquity and the transience of glory. More than a century later, when Alan Moore rewrote Ozymandias in Watchmen, Shelley's ruined king was transformed into a morally ambiguous antagonist with the ambition to construct a new global saviour myth capable of uniting humanity. Moore's self-fashioned Ozymandias also evokes the myth of Superman, a figure that can be traced to Friedrich Nietzsche's concept (1883) of Übermensch (beyond-human). From Nietzschean philosophical ideal of self-overcoming, the Superman later takes forms in different myths: George Bernard Shaw's play and most famously in Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster's comics, where Superman represents the experiences and aspirations of Jewish immigrant communities before being incorporated into American national mythology during WWII and the Cold War. Superman mythmaking also transcended across the Pacific. In postwar Japan, superhumans like Astro-Boy and Ultraman reconstructed the archetype into social recovery and national renewal in the aftermath of atomic destruction. These examples show that mythmaking reinvents cultural symbols into new stories in response to political realities and collective memory. While myths are traditionally framed as archaic narratives of gods and heroes, modern scholars argue that the act of mythmaking can act as a mobilizing force in society and serves as a political power beyond its presence in art (Citton 2025; Josephson-Storm 2017). A political myth operates as a system of explanation, providing a cryptography through which the disconcerting chaos of contemporary facts is ordered and understood (Girardet 1987; Segal 2020). By offering an imaginary reading of a historical moment, myths restore intelligibility to a fractured world, manifesting in recurring structures like the nostalgia for a Golden Age or the yearning for a providential Saviour. However, this phenomenological reality of worldbuilding parallels Walter D. Mignolo's decolonial critique of "enunciation," where the content of myth is disseminated by the enunciator who ultimately possesses power (2018, 144-145).?? Mythmaking is still an ongoing cultural process without a singular definition. In a way, its study can be viewed as a consequence of the emergence of anthropology, which, during the 19th century, inquired about the concept of myth. This was the work of, for example, E.B. Tylor and J.G. Frazer. Yet, they were not so concerned about the aesthetics of mythmaking, as they viewed it as a form of "primitive knowledge" that was the exact opposite of Western art and science. Across the 20th century, authors as diverse as Bronislaw Malinowski (1922), Ernst Cassirer (1946), Claude Lévi-Strauss (1978), Northrop Frye (1967), Carl Jung (1964), Joseph Campbell (2004), and Mircea Eliade (1954) have suggested a whole range of different and often conflictive definitions for this concept. They actively engaged with the knowledge traditions of anthropology, philosophy, history, comparative literature, and religion studies.? One compelling form of analyzing mythmaking emerged at the intersection of aesthetics, philosophy, politics, and critical theory during the 19th century. Reacting against Enlightenment rationalism, German Romantics and Idealists such as Schiller, Schelling, and Hegel called for a "new mythology" to heal the alienation between humanity and nature while birthing the philosophical myth of absence-the belief that modernity is uniquely "mythless" (Josephson-Storm 2017, 17-21). This tension is central to the work of Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno, who, echoing Max Weber, argued that the Enlightenment's "disenchantment of the world" sought to dispel myths through reason, yet ultimately revealed that "enlightenment reverts to mythology" (2016, xviii), as instrumental rationality facilitated the domination of human beings over one another. In this way, inquiring the aesthetics of mythmaking involves a critique of different areas of the socio-cultural construct, reaching the realms of narrative, culture, and power.?? Amidst these diverse intellectual traditions and definitions of mythmaking, this call invites contributions that explore mythmaking as an ongoing process of cultural translation, forms of exercising power, political representation, and artistic (re)creation. We are interested in examining how mythmaking is still continually making, remaking, and mobilising new meanings and identities across historical periods, cultural contexts, and media forms. Proposals for thematic articles in response to this call are welcome, including but not limited to the following topics: ? Mythmaking and memory retelling? ? Superstition, hagiographies, and religion stories?? ? Mythmaking in different culturalforms: films, comics, and music? ? Mythmaking and Nationmaking?? ? Mythmaking as Tools of (De)colonial Discourse?? ? Mythmaking and Identity: theInvention of Tradition and Self-making? ? Mythmaking and Imaginary?? ? Lived experience and Phenomenology of Mythmaking ? The Power of Mythmaking in Social and Political Contexts? ? Mysticism and Poetry? ? Myth and Mythmaking in Literature from Romanticism to Modernism? ? Mythopoesia? ? Women Writers/Poets and Feminist Revisionist Mythmaking? ? The Role of Mythmaking in Visual Arts? ? The Study of Mythography in Modern Culture? ? Mythic ecology? ? Mythmaking, Philosophy, and Science: from myth to reason? ? Mythmaking and Psychology (Jungian Psychology, Psychoanalysis, etc)? Submissions and review process Abstracts will be received and reviewed by the Diffractions editorial board who will decide on the pertinence of proposals for the upcoming issue. After submission, we will get in touch with the authors of accepted abstracts in order to invite them to submit a full article. However, this does not imply that these papers will be automatically published. Rather, they will go through a peer-review process that will determine whether papers are publishable with minor or major changes, or they do not fulfil the criteria for publication.? Please send abstracts of 150 to 250 words, and 5-8 keywords by October 31, 2026, to info. diffractions@gmail.com with the subject "Diffractions 13", followed by your last name.? The full papers should be submitted by January 31, 2026, through the journal's platform, using our Style Sheet: https://revistas.ucp. pt/index.php/diffractions/ about/submissions.? Every issue of Diffractions has a thematic focus but also contains special sections for non-thematic articles. If you are interested in submitting an article that is not related to the topic of this issue, please consult the general guidelines available on the Diffractions website at https://revistas.ucp.pt/ index.php/diffractions/about/ submissions. The submission and review process for non-thematic articles is the same as for the general thematic issue. All research areas of the humanities are welcome, and we accept contributions in English or Portuguese.? References: Adorno, Theodor W., and Max Horkheimer. 2016. items.fullDescription: THE SIXTIES Call for proposals: Papers, Sessions, Panels Popular Culture Association Annual Conference March 24-27, 2027 in Boston, MA The Sixties area of the Popular Culture Association welcomes submissions for papers and presentations on any aspect of popular culture from the era. Topics of interest might include, but are not limited to: Film, television, radio, and other media (underground press, posters, etc.) Analysis of influential books/authors, art/artists, films/filmmakers, etc. New developments in religion and spirituality Psychedelia and its many manifestations The sexual revolution Music and fashion, as cultural expression and/or consumer culture New social arrangements, e.g., communes, back to the land movement 1968 or other significant dates, places, or events, e.g., Freedom Summer, Days of Rage, etc. Countercultural movements, e.g., hippies, Diggers, SDS, Black Panther Party, White Panther Party, etc.Politics and protests of the era, e.g., Civil Rights, Vietnam War, Free Speech Movement, etc. Race and gender issues, e.g., Black Power, women's rights, etc. Media representations of/reactions to any of the above Rock music, the counterculture, or other developments in international/global contexts (i.e. outside the US and UK) The significance of the decade in contemporary society and culture, including ongoing debates and revised perspectives NOTE : This year PCA is trying out a wider shared theme for the conference, on the general subject of "Revolutions and Revisions in Popular Culture" - which obviously connects with many Sixties topics. As part of that theme, presenters are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, technological change, or changing cultural practices. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. ALSO : This year we are also featuring a joint panel between the Sixties area and the Radio, Podcast, and Sound Media area. Possible paper topics are wide open, and could include things like: the FM radio revolution in the U.S. (freeform/progressive formats, changes in FCC policies, etc.); significant radio stations, such as WDIA in Memphis, KSAN in San Francisco, etc.; "pirate radio" in the U.K. (Radio Caroline, etc.) and official responses (the creation of BBC1, etc.); the expansion of stereophonic audio in relation to popular music, psychedelic rock, etc.; the influence of/by particular record labels on pop culture and the counterculture (especially independents such as Motown, Vanguard, ESP, etc.); more recent podcasts or other audio media about the 1960s; any of the above in non-U.S./U.K. contexts; and any other related subjects. If you would like your paper submission to be considered for the shared panel(s), please note that on your abstract or via email to the area chair. DEADLINE FOR SUBMISSIONS: October 31, 2026. For individual papers, please submit a title and 300-word abstract. Be sure to proofread your name, title, and abstract closely as this text will become part of the program should your proposal be accepted. All proposals should be submitted online via the PCA/ACA website: http://pcaaca.org More information about the submission process can be found here: https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines Inquiries about possible papers or proposals for round table sessions or full panels (including those involving the conference theme mentioned above) are also welcomed and encouraged. For themed paper sessions, each presenter must enter her/his own presentation and then contact the area chair to assemble them into a panel. All presenters must be current members of the PCA in order to submit, and must register for the conference in order to present. More detailed information about various conference matters can be found at: https://pcaaca.org/page/2027conf and elsewhere on the PCA website (check the site menus for specific topics). Please feel free to get in touch if you have any questions about topics, process, or the conference in general. Kevin M. items.title: Irony: Dramatic and Otherwise
items.location: University of Tübingen, Germany · Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate
items.excerpt: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it e...
items.fullDescription: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it evokes and reflects basic constituents of human communication: in particular, the relationship between what is said and what is meant and the relationship between what is said and what is known. Irony comes into play when these relationships are marked by significant discrepancies. The discrepancy between what is said and what is meant is essential for verbal irony and the discrepancy between what is said and what is known is fundamental to dramatic (or narrative) irony. If and how these two kinds of irony belong together, however, is a moot point and one of the questions to be addressed by our symposium. Thus the unequal distribution of knowledge (between characters and/or between characters and the reader) which marks narrative and dramatic irony may be related to the divergence which characterizes verbal irony. When Viola in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, disguised as a boy, says to Orsino: "I am all the daughters of my father's house," Orsino, who believes Viola to be a young man, must regard this statement as verbal irony on Viola's part. What is said ("daughters") is very different from what appears to be meant ("sons"). To us, the audience, however, this is a case of dramatic irony since we know that Viola is a woman and we observe Orsino's ignorance. What makes this case particularly intriguing is that here dramatic irony is not based on a discrepancy between what is said and what we know since Viola literally speaks the truth. The discrepancy arises between what we know and what is supposed to be spoken ironically. The example shows that asking about the relationship between verbal and dramatic/narrative irony entails numerous other questions that the Connotations symposium is going to address. In particular, we will ask about effects of irony, both with regard to characters and the audience. What is the added value of an ironic remark? What does it tell us about the speaker? In what way does an ironic utterance signal that there is a common ground between the communication partners? Are the inclusion and exclusion of others, i.e. those who get the ironical meaning and those who don't, similar to cases of discrepant awareness? How do we know that an utterance is meant ironically and how are we to deal with ambiguity in this respect? Can non-verbal irony markers be encoded in literary texts? Are theories of verbal irony based on notions of echo and pretence relatable to drama and fiction? We invite papers focussing on these and related questions, based on literature in English from the Middle Ages to the present. Please send an abstract (300 words max.) to the editors of Connotations at symposium2027@connotations.de by 31 October 2026

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). items.excerpt: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. items.fullDescription: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. In this way, the theory provides the “genus” of which a given film will be a mere “species”. The application of psychoanalytic ideas or Marxist concepts to film would therefore run the risk of depriving the specificity and singularity of the object in favour of the hegemony of the theory. Here, theory would truly live up to its theological vocation (the “theo” in theory refers to God) standing transcendentally above its “object” upon which it would cast its daunting shadow.

items.title: Travelling Cultural Heritage. Circulation and Digital Afterlives
items.location: Sibiu, Romania · Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu
items.excerpt: Travelling Cultural Heritage Circulation and Digital Afterlives Call for Papers Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference 4th edition Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Romania December 10-11, 2026 Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, as part of the FORTHEM Alliance, invites scholars, researchers, and practitioners to submit proposals for the 4th edition...
items.fullDescription: Travelling Cultural Heritage Circulation and Digital Afterlives Call for Papers Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference 4th edition Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Romania December 10-11, 2026 Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, as part of the FORTHEM Alliance, invites scholars, researchers, and practitioners to submit proposals for the 4th edition of the Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference, dedicated to exploring cultural heritage as a dynamic process of circulation across cultural, geographical, institutional, and historical boundaries. The 2026 edition focuses on Travelling Cultural Heritage (TCH): an approach that understands heritage not as a fixed repository, but as a process through which cultural forms, practices, ideas, and meanings move, encounter different contexts, and are transformed along the way. Drawing on Edward Said's concept of "travelling theory", Mieke Bal's "travelling concepts", and scholarship on cultural circulation, TCH shifts attention from mobile objects to the processes through which heritage is transmitted, adapted, appropriated, reinterpreted, and re-signified. Heritage travels through migration, exchange, conquest, education, trade, tourism, collecting, translation, transmedial transfer, and institutional networks. Migrants adapt cultural practices acquired abroad to their home contexts; travelling elites import fashions, recipes, and other cultural products; artistic styles acquire regional forms as they circulate; and networks of institutions, scholars, dealers, and historical circumstances determine how artefacts enter major collections. Such movements involve adaptation and transformation, but also appropriation, exclusion, and unequal centre-periphery relations. Circulation may allow heritage to acquire new meanings, but it may also entail loss. The large-scale purchase, digitisation, and destruction of books for AI training suggests a future in which physical heritage disappears while its digital avatars survive-an extreme form of travel across media and material states, combining virtual preservation with material destruction. More optimistically, AI, data science, interoperable infrastructures, and spatial visualisation can trace cultural circulation, compare contexts, and recover seemingly lost artefacts, including previously unreadable ancient manuscripts. We welcome contributions that engage with Travelling Cultural Heritage from disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives, including cultural and heritage studies, anthropology, archaeology, sociology, history, linguistics and literary studies, political science, art history, architecture, digital humanities, economics, media studies, religious studies, drama, film, the performing arts, museum studies, memory studies, and food studies . Contributors are invited to submit abstracts on, but not limited to, the following themes: Travelling Cultural Heritage: theories, concepts, and methodologies; Cultural circulation, transmission, adaptation, and re-signification; Heritage: migration, displacement, and diaspora; Museums, collections, objects, routes, networks, intermediaries, and infrastructures of cultural circulation; The movement of architectural forms, artistic practices, rituals, and cultural traditions; Colonial, postcolonial, and decolonial circulations of cultural heritage; Digital heritage, digital infrastructures, AI, platforms and computational approaches to cultural circulation; Heritage in translation: what changes when cultural forms travel between languages and the production of new heritage meanings Local content, foreign forms: adaptation and naturalisation across literatures; World Cultural Heritage: comparative approaches to heritage beyond national frameworks; Archaeological evidence for mobility, exchange, and cultural contacts; Memory and heritage: overlappings and differences; Case studies of cultural forms, practices, objects, ideas, or meanings that have travelled across contexts. Submission Guidelines Please submit an abstract of 250-300 words , along with a short biographical note ( max. 100 words ), to Ovio Olaru ( ovio.olaru@ulbsibiu.ro ) and Daniela Stanciu-P?sc?ri?a ( daniela.stanciu@ulbsibiu.ro ) by November 1, 2026. The organisers' decision regarding submissions will be communicated by November 15. For effectiveness, please include " Cultural Heritage Lab conference submission " in the subject line of your email. The conference will be held in English, German, and French, and will take place exclusively on-site. We look forward to your contributions! Kind regards, The organisers

items.location: · PopMeC Association for US Popular Culture Studies
items.excerpt: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. Television series, films, vide...
items.fullDescription: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. Television series, films, videogames, TikTokers, podcasters, memes and other forms of digital culture reach global audiences and shape political identities and cultural imaginaries. Far from being mere entertainment, these texts have consequently become intertwined and virtually inseparable from the daily practices through which individuals get their news input and even their education. The purpose of this year's virtual conference is to open a space for the analysis of the ethical principles (or lack thereof) that seem to guide the construction, circulation and reception of public discourses within the popular culture ecosystem, including both more traditional mediums such as television and comics, but also the products that emerge from generative AI. Popular media content exists as a key source of information in public discourse and influences how we interpret contemporary political issues, how we teach and learn, and even how we exist and behave in society. Although media effects have long been proven to be negotiated rather than direct, the understanding of desirable aesthetics, mindless entertainment and the rhetoric used in political discussions have been hugely impacted by AI generated content. With this cultural media environment in mind, this virtual conference invites explorations of US popular culture through the perspective of media ethics, media literacy and aesthetics. We aim at establishing a space of discussion on the political, educational, ethical and social implications of contemporary media consumption through the analysis of US popular culture. The conference welcomes contributions that tackle the ethical dimensions and societal impact of US popular culture across a wide range of media forms and how they operate within the fragmented and algorithmically curated media ecosystem that we inhabit. We welcome analysis of both mainstream and independent productions, historical and contemporary texts, as well as emerging digital practices. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: × Media ethics and the social responsibilities of producers, platforms and audiences × Media literacy as a framework for analyzing contemporary popular culture × Popular culture as a case study for developing media literacy, ethical reasoning and critical thinking in education × The teaching potential behind popular media texts × Media effects and audience reception of US popular culture × Social media trends, influencers and memes × AI aesthetics in popular media × Polarization, misinformation, conspiracy narratives, and the circulation of disinformation through popular media × (Un)ethical representation of minorities × Political communication, civic engagement, and democratic participation through entertainment media × Representation of political and social problems in US popular culture Deadline for proposals: 1 November 2026 We accept abstract proposals for individual presentations (≈ 250 words), as well as full panels (3 presenters, ≈ 250-word description of the panel plus brief abstracts of all papers). Please, submit your abstract proposal via email at popmec.media@gmail.com as a single attachment (.doc, .docx, .odt) including name, affiliation (if any), and contact email.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: [Children's and Young Adult Literature] at CEA 2027 Apr. 1-3, 2027 | St. Louis, Missouri The Westin St. Louis Hotel https://cea-web.org/the-conference-hotel The College English Association, a gathering of scholar-teachers in English studies, welcomes proposals for presentations on Children's and Young Adult Literature for our 57th annual conference. Submit your proposal at www.cea-web.org Scholars and teachers of children's and YA lit intimately know the transformative power the right story at the right time can have on an elementary, middle, or high school student. We do not need reminding of how words, and how they are communicated, to young learners have the ability to grow cognitive processes and lead to future generations of lovers of the written word and future torchbearers of the significance of those words coming from the minds of human beings. Coalescing around the conference theme, we consider how the influence of diverse sculpted stories opens the door to deeper discernment across the curriculum. Conference Theme: Gateways For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Tracing its history back to French explorers in the second half of the 18th century, the great city of St. Louis began as a fur trading post named after King Louis IX of France and was established on the ancestral lands of the Osage Nation, Missouria, and Illini Confederacy. Becoming part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the city famously came to be known as the "Gateway to the West," serving as a launching point for generations of explorers and settlers expanding the frontier. Yet, we must remember that the city also serves as a gateway to its past as part of indigenous lands transformed through its colonial history into a major river port and trading center that fostered migration both outwards and inwards for centuries. Today, St. Louis invites us to reflect on the continued significance of gateways in our 21st-century lives. GENERAL CALL FOR PAPERS GATEWAYS: For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Potential areas of interest: How do gateways expand literary and cultural spaces but also, as access points, mark out boundaries and limits? Do gateways invite gatekeepers to enable and limit access? Is it possible to imagine gateways without gatekeepers? How can we imagine literary and cultural gateways to foster inter-cultural, cross-cultural, and trans-cultural interactions? How do we envision pedagogical approaches to create gateways for our students to new literary vistas, critical thought, and professional opportunities? How can gateways in both their physical and symbolic significances (like the city of St. Louis and the Gateway Arch) connect the territorial to the cultural, imaginative, and spiritual in literary-critical studies? In what ways can we re-imagine our scholarly and pedagogical work to open up interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary gateways? For CEA 2027, we are especially interested topics related to GATEWAYS in texts, disciplines, people, cultural studies, media, and pedagogy. Consider such topics as the implications of political gateways across time and place, cultural gateways of identity, gateways in the media (including social media) and how they impact society, pedagogical gateways of teaching philosophy and their implementation, or personal gateways through autobiography and memoir. GENERAL TOPICS: The CEA Conference encompasses a wide range of areas, including literary studies, creative writing, rhetoric and composition, technical communication, linguistics, and film. We further encourage proposals in areas about our wider role as academics, including student/instructor accountability and assessment, student advising, academic leadership in departments and programs, and the place of the English department in the university. NEW FOR 2027: UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. For additional information or discussion about this topic and its panels, please contact Peter Elliott at pselliott@anderson.edu.

items.fullDescription: The Whorfian invites pitches from writers, artists, translators, scholars, and close observers of everyday life. We look for clear, attentive pieces that show how language shapes what people notice, understand, make, or miss-across culture, translation, psychology, philosophy, anthropology, art, music, literature, and lived experience. We do not accept full manuscripts, press releases, or pitches already under consideration elsewhere. We especially invite concise pitches for features, which are our usual commissioned format, as well as shorter Traces, essays, and edited conversations. A good pitch is 150-250 words: the idea, why it fits The Whorfian, the format, one or two sources or examples, and a short bio. Authors retain copyright. The Whorfian's editors welcome your pitches and inquiries. Please wait at least one week before asking about a pitch you have already sent. Our editorial meetings review pitches that meet the criteria above, and we respond to everyone who follows them. Unsolicited manuscripts may not be considered; please contact us first to discuss your subject and framing. Traces - 700-750 wordsA precise, compact reading of a small cluster of elements in context-a set of expressions, a palette, symbols, or a few lines-and what they reveal about the wider scene. Whorfian essays - 1,200-1,800 wordsOur principal format: one strong argument, supported by research, examples, and clear prose. Features - 2,000-3,000 wordsLonger essays, interviews, or reported cultural analyses, commissioned selectively. Conversations - 1,000-1,600 edited wordsAn interview shaped into a coherent exchange, not a raw transcript. While we operate as a small publication, we are committed to paying our writers and offer a standard contributor honorarium (currently $75, $125, and $200 depending on your submission type) for accepted pieces. Only the authors of successful pitches will be contacted.

items.fullDescription: Confound the Time welcomes papers that investigate the ways in which texts, objects, and images from the medieval and early modern periods re-envision and reconstruct the past or imagine and anticipate the future. We also welcome papers that explore the ways in which medieval and early modern artifacts, history, and culture are reimagined and reconstructed in later periods. As part of our commitment to accessibility, Confound the Time will be entirely virtual and have no registration fee. Graduate students and early career scholars are especially encouraged to submit. Topics for individual papers may include: Medieval and early modern reception of classical mythology/culture Early modern reception of medieval literature/culture The Pre-Raphaelites and other neo-medievalist movements Contemporary video games, graphic novels, television shows, and/or films with medieval or early modern settings, characters, and cultures Dungeons and Dragons and/or other role-playing or tabletop games Manuscript Studies/Book History Time/The Times Gender and Sexuality Nationalism and Race Papers that address these subjects are encouraged, but any paper that centers on medieval or early modern studies will be considered. Please fill out this form to the best of your ability in order to submit: https://forms.gle/B8YhxejNzQHGsfcV8 The deadline for all abstract submissions is November 7th, 2026. The virtual conference will be held from February 6th-February 7th 2027. Questions can be directed to Drs. Audrey Gradzewicz (U of Wisconsin-Madison) and Audrey Saxton (Bethany College, KS) at confoundthetime@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: The First International Conference "Genealogies of Healing: Nineteenth-Century Hispanic Culture and Dialogues with Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean in the Digital Age" will be held on March 29-31, 2027, at the University of Costa Rica, Western Campus (Sede de Occidente). This international academic event seeks to bring together researchers, academics, artists, educators, and professionals from different disciplines to explore the historical, cultural, social, artistic, scientific, and technological dimensions of healing and well-being. The Congress proposes a dialogue between nineteenth-century traditions and contemporary approaches to health and healing, examining continuities, transformations, exchanges, and tensions across the Hispanic world, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Particular attention will be given to the ways in which literature, art, spirituality, traditional medicine, bodily practices, digital technologies, and community experiences have shaped understandings and practices of healing. Suggested themes include: Genealogies of Healing in Nineteenth-Century Hispanic Culture Representations of Illness in Nineteenth-Century Literature and the Press Art and Healing: Music, Dance, Painting, and Theatre as Therapeutic Practices Dialogues between Allopathic Medicine and Traditional Healing Systems Spirituality, Religion, and Healing Practices Healing through Words: Narratives, Discourse, and Therapeutic Processes Convergences between Bodily Practices (Yoga, Pranayama, Sports) and Holistic Health Healing Traditions in Asia and the Caribbean: Exchanges with the Hispanic World Digital Health, Applications, Platforms, and Well-Being Monitoring Ethical and Clinical Risks of Chatbots and Mental Health Technologies Social Media, Virality, and Their Impact on Emotional Health Attention, Cognition, and Technology Digital Churches, the Spiritual Economy, and New Forms of Religiosity Education and Well-Being Public Health Policies in Digital and Multicultural Environments Interdisciplinarity in Health: Intersections between Art, Science, and Technology Imaginaries of Good and Evil in Processes of Illness and Healing Community Well-Being and Territorial Experiences Researchers interested in participating are invited to submit proposals in accordance with the Congress guidelines. For further information, submission guidelines, and updates, please visit the official Congress website

items.fullDescription: In the 2000s and 2010s, social networking facilitated citizen-based activism of enormous significance like #BlackLivesMatter and #MeToo. But in the 2020s, corporate enshittification and government surveillance have restricted the reach of social networking tools. For example, Elon Musk’s purchase of Twitter meant that many users left X rather than adapt their activist practices to the restrictive corporate environment (Tenbarge & Collier 2024). Instances such as the Trump administration’s use of social media posts to target international students during the Gaza protests caused many users to avoid social media altogether (Lonas Cochran 2025).

items.fullDescription: CFP: 28th Southeast Conference for Languages, Literatures, and Film (Feb 27-28, 2027) in St. Petersburg, Florida (on the University of South Florida St. Petersburg Campus) Languages and Cultures in a Changing World: Identity, Responsibility, and Justice Abstracts for papers (and panels) are now being considered. Deadline for abstracts: Nov. 16, 2026 Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. To view prior publication, visit the conference website. The SCFLLF welcomes papers on all aspects of literature, theoretical and applied linguistics, culture, philosophy, cultural history, film, other popular media, second language acquisition, and language pedagogy pertaining to non-English languages (ancient and modern). We would like to encourage (but not limit) submissions addressing our conference theme: Identity, Responsibility and Justice, in its broadest understanding. Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. The humanities and the study of languages are facing changing institutional and social expectations. These changes encourage us to reconsider what work we do and the people and communities our work serves. To whom and to what, are artists, scholars and teachers accountable? How do languages, literatures, films, and other forms of cultural expression preserve or challenge established narratives and structures? How do they engage with different identities? How can they help us understand the present and/or imagine different futures? What responsibilities come with teaching and learning languages as well as with studying, interpreting, and representing other cultures? This conference invites scholars working in non-English languages, literatures, film and media, cultural studies, applied and theoretical linguistics, second-language acquisition, and language pedagogy to explore these and related questions from a wide range of disciplinary, theoretical, historical, and methodological perspectives. The conference theme, Identity, Responsibility, and Justice, is deliberately broad. Responsibility may involve our relationships with students and communities, with texts and their histories, with linguistic and cultural traditions, or with the institutions in which we teach and conduct research. Or responsibility can be interrogated with regard to artists and art, in a broad sense. Justice can also be approached in diverse ways. It may involve social justice, questions of representation and recognition, historical memory, inclusion and exclusion, or access and lack thereof to language learning. Justice may also concern translation and cultural mediation or the ways in which literature, film, language, and other cultural practices engage with conflict, inequality, trauma, discrimination, displacement, and/or social change. The SCFLLF keynote speaker is Adam Schwartz (Associate Professor of Language, Culture & Society, Oregon State University). Dr. Schwartz's research addresses Spanish language education and Spanish-English multilingualisms in the U.S. He takes particular interest in intersections of language, race and racism, wherein questions of identity, responsibility and justice persist. In addition to various articles and chapters, he has authored three books. These include Spanish So White: Conversations on the Inconvenient Racism of a 'Foreign' Language Education (2023). He is also the co-author of Aquí se habla: Centering the Local and Personal in Spanish Language Education (2025) as well as Language, Identity and Justice: The Anthropolitical Worlds of Ana Celia Zentella (2026). Some suggestions of topics and their artistic representations include: identity, responsibility, and justice represented in literature, art, film, and other forms of popular media, including social media influence of film and literature on the public and private sphere reassessing the purpose and value of language teaching expressions and perceptions of trauma in response to injustice justice in utopian fictional worlds addressing and expressing identity in the language classroom questions of identity in literature, film, the arts, and other popular media responsibility issues in production and reception of artistic expressions responsibilities associated with researching and representing cultures apart or in comparison to our own the broader influence of imaginary worlds created in film, literature, the visual arts, and other forms of media on real political and personal justice language and linguistic-related topics concerning identity, responsibility, and justice other topics Please submit a proposal (of no more than 250 words) for a single paper or a full panel (max. of 3 presentations) on the conference webpage. We can only accept online submissions. Please contact Margit Grieb (grieber@usf.edu) if you have any questions.

items.excerpt: “Culture,” notes Raymond Williams, “is one of the two or three most complicated words in the English language” (87). items.fullDescription: “Culture,” notes Raymond Williams, “is one of the two or three most complicated words in the English language” (87). Its etymological root in cultivation—the tending and propagation of life—signals a resistance to being contained. Classroom pedagogy encompasses various elements into it—mythology, rituals, religion, tradition; movies, songs, literature; fashion, food, art—classifying it as ‘a whole way of life.’ Yet, culture surpasses being merely a way of life; it represents a way of understanding life and saturating existence with meaning. In the 19th Century, Matthew Arnold viewed culture as a framework supporting liberal humanist ideology, which aimed to prescribe a universal definition of excellence.

items.fullDescription: At many universities, learning communities foster connectedness and belonging among students. Learning communities are typically composed of cohorts of students taking aligned first-year classes, but they take many other forms as well. At their best, they promote the perspective that learning is a collective activity in which knowledge is constructed through relationships with peers, professors, and communities, bringing together diverse voices and interdisciplinary perspectives. They provide a welcoming environment that eases the transition to college and provides a foundation for a peer network of academic support (Schreiber & Valle, 2013).

items.fullDescription: Overview | South Mediterranean University, Tunisia Hybrid Format: In-person and Online Participation The SMU Conference on AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms will take place at South Mediterranean University, Tunisia. This research oriented event brings together scholars, educators, instructional designers, and researchers to explore evidence-based pedagogical innovation in technology-mediated and AI-enhanced learning environments. This conference provides an international platform to present academic research, foster interdisciplinary dialogue, and advance collaboration on the future of teaching and learning in the AI era. The 2027 SMU Conference, themed "AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms," examines how AI and emerging educational technologies reshape instructional design, classroom engagement, assessment, and learning ecosystems. Key focus areas include measurable learning outcomes, ethical and inclusive AI integration, pedagogical quality assurance, and student competency development in hybrid and digital environments. We invite researchers, practitioners, instructional designers, and graduate students worldwide to submit original research, empirical studies, and case studies on innovative pedagogy, AI-enhanced instruction, learning analytics, engagement strategies, and inclusive practices.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Volume 37, Issue 1 & 2 (2027) Dear Colleagues, Litera: Journal of Language, Literature and Culture Studies - Dil, Edebiyat ve Kültür Ara?t?rmalar? Dergisi, the official publication of the Department of Western Languages and Literatures at Istanbul University, invites submissions for its 2026 issues (Volume 36, Issues 1 & 2). An open-access, peer-reviewed, and multilingual journal published twice a year (June & December), Litera is indexed in ELSEVIER SCOPUS, Web of Science ESCI, MLA International Bibliography, DOAJ (Directory of Open Access Journals), ERIH PLUS, EBSCO Communication Source, EBSCO Central & Eastern European Academic Source, Gale Cengage and Ulrichsweb. While our core focus remains on literary studies, linguistics, and cultural studies, we welcome interdisciplinary approaches that combine literary and linguistic analysis with insights from cultural theory and media studies-provided they maintain a clear relevance to our aim and scope We welcome original research articles that engage with current debates and critical issues in the study of Western (American, English, French, Belgian, German, Swiss, Austrian, Italian, Spanish, Latin American and Modern Greek) languages, literatures, and cultures. In particular, we encourage contributions that reflect cutting-edge scholarship in areas such as, but not limited to: · Contemporary literary theory · Disability Studies · Human-Animal Studies · Posthumanism and critical posthumanities · Ecofeminism and ecocriticism · Ecosemiotics and Ecolinguistics · Discourse Studies · Intersectional and decolonial approaches · Digital humanities and media theory · Film Studies · Medieval Studies · Posthuman Communication Studies · Gender studies · Narrative and identity in contemporary fiction · Transnationalism and migration literature · Crete studies Submission Windows: · Issue 1 (June 2027): November 1-30, 2026 · Issue 2 (December 2027): May 1-31, 2027 Submission Guidelines: Manuscripts must be original, unpublished, and not under review elsewhere. Re-use of thesis content, dissertations, or previously published conference material is not permitted. All submissions are subject to a double-blind peer reviewprocess. Languages of Publication: English, German, French, Italian, and Spanish No processing or publication fees. Eligibility: Submissions are accepted from authors who hold a PhD. items.title: Hong Kong Temporalities
items.location: Online · Chinese University of Hong Kong
items.fullDescription: [???????????????? ???????????? ????????????????????????????????????] ???????????????? ???????????????? ????????????????????????????????????????????????????: ????????????????????, ????????????????????????????????, ???????????? ???????????????????????????? A Hong Kong Studies Virtual Symposium 21-22 January 2027 | Online ???????????????????????????????? ???????????? ???????????????? ???????????? ???????????????????????????????????? ????????????????: https://bit.ly/4hGfW8y Organised by Hong Kong Studies, this two-day symposium invites papers from across the humanities and social sciences that explore time and temporality in relation to Hong Kong's cultural, historical, technological, social and political imaginaries. Hong Kong has long been a city peculiarly conscious of time. Its modern history has been narrated through beginnings and endings, leases and deadlines, arrivals and departures, anniversaries and countdowns. 1997 became an anticipated future long before it became history; 2047 likewise exists simultaneously as date, horizon, projection and cultural imaginary. Yet Hong Kong's temporalities extend far beyond these emblematic dates. They can be found in memories of vanished places, family histories and memoirs, experiences of migration and exile, changing generations and languages, speculative and science-fictional futures, technological acceleration, artificial intelligence, and everyday experiences of waiting, repetition, anticipation and change. The symposium asks: what forms of time have shaped Hong Kong and its cultural imagination? How are its pasts remembered, forgotten, recovered or reinvented? How do memoir, literature, cinema, art and popular culture create alternative relationships between past, present and future? What temporalities emerge through migration, diaspora, exile and return? How do generations inhabit historical time differently? What happens to experiences of time under conditions of rapid political, urban and technological transformation? How might artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies alter our understanding of memory, prediction, authorship and futurity? And what can science fiction and speculative practices tell us about Hong Kong futures that have been anticipated, deferred, foreclosed or not yet imagined? We welcome papers addressing topics including, but not limited to, countdowns and deadlines; history and historiography; memory and forgetting; memoir and life writing; nostalgia and post-nostalgia; futurity and anticipation; science fiction and speculative fiction; utopia and dystopia; technology and technological change; artificial intelligence and algorithmic time; digital memory and archives; ageing and generational time; migration, diaspora, exile and return; colonial and postcolonial temporalities; urban transformation and disappearing spaces; everyday rhythms, waiting and repetition; acceleration and rupture; haunting, spectrality and afterlives; alternative histories and counterfutures; and temporality in literature, cinema, music, visual art, performance and popular culture. By bringing these approaches into conversation, the symposium seeks to consider Hong Kong as a site of intersecting temporalities, where remembered pasts, contested presents and multiple possible futures continually reshape one another. We invite contributions from scholars at all stages of their professional development, as well as independent scholars, writers, artists, filmmakers, critics, curators, educators, technologists, and other cultural practitioners whose work engages with Hong Kong and questions of temporality. In addition to traditional academic papers, the symposium welcomes short presentations or informal talks that approach Hong Kong temporalities through creative, professional, personal, or interdisciplinary perspectives. Please submit an abstract of 300-500 words, along with a short third-person biography (approx. 150 words), compiled in a single Word document. Submissions should be sent tohkstudiesjournal@gmail.com by ???????????????????????? ???? ???????????????????????????????? ????????????????. Following the symposium, selected papers (6,000-8,000 words) will be considered for publication in future issues of Hong Kong Studies (Open Journals Hub).

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers Yearbook KRIEG UND LITERATUR/WAR AND LITERATURE VOL. 32 (2027) (Göttingen: V&R unipress/Universitätsverlag Osnabrückpublished since 1989 and as a yearbook since 2000; distributed to subscribers worldwide) Invisible Fronts - Representations of War between AI, Disinformation, and Hybrid Warfare Wars have never been fought solely on military battlefields. Cyber operations, social media, automated weapons systems, algorithmic decision-making processes, and generative artificial intelligence have transformed warfare in recent decades-as well as its media representation and public perception. Disinformation, surveillance, and the deliberate manipulation of public perception are increasingly blurring the lines between war and peace, reality and simulation, and documentation and staging. The 2027 issue of KRIEG UND LITERATUR/WAR AND LITERATURE explores cultural representations of these developments. The focus is on how 20th- and 21st-century media depict, reflect on, critique, or anticipate technological and hybrid forms of warfare, and how new technologies are changing the conditions under which wars are narrated, documented, remembered, and perceived as real. Possible topics include: • AI, autonomous weapons systems, drones, and algorithmic targeting; • cyberwarfare, hybrid warfare, and digital infrastructures; • propaganda, disinformation, and deepfakes; • generative AI and synthetic images of war; • manipulation of perception, memory, and enemy stereotypes; • responsibility and agency in the relationship between humans and machines; • historical imaginaries of automated and hybrid warfare. Across all genres and formats, contributions may examine works and materials from literature, film and television, comics and graphic novels, visual and digital art, photography, social media, and video games. Interdisciplinary, comparative, and transnational approaches are also welcome. Contributions may be submitted in German or English . The following general formatting guidelines should be observed: • Submit as a WORD or RTF document; language: German or English; a maximum of 25 A4 pages (excluding illustrations); Footnotes rather than endnotes); • Figures (printed in black and white) must be submitted separately as offset film, a reproducible original, or in digital format (*.tif, *.jpg with at least 300 dpi in CMYK mode). Please mark the location in the text where each figure is to appear. Do not embed the figures in the document; • Include correct and complete figure captions in the text or in a separate file; • Authors are responsible for obtaining all necessary reproduction permissions. Detailed "Guidelines for Authors" will be sent separately. Abstracts : 1,500-2,000 characters (including spaces) Deadline for abstract submissions : December 31, 2026 Notification of acceptance : January 31, 2027 Deadline for full paper submission : June 30, 2027 Paper length : 15-25 pages Contact and Submission : Claudia Junk, M.A. and Alice Cadeddu, M.A. (Editors) Email: junk@osnabrueck.de; cadeddu@osnabrueck.de Erich Maria Remarque Peace Center; www.remarque.de

items.title: Animal Studies Across Disciplines
items.location: Arizona State University · Arizona State University
items.excerpt: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pe...
items.fullDescription: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pervasive pollution. The effects of the Anthropocene have been caused by only a small percentage of the world's population, yet those living in the Global South disproportionately suffer the consequences. The Anthropocene, then, is just as much a social problem as it is an environmental issue. Despite the centrality of animals to planetary health, however, nonhuman life often remains peripheral to discussions of climate and environmental sustainability, even as industrial agriculture drives deforestation and carbon emissions, species extinction destabilizes ecosystems, and the increasing emergence of zoonotic diseases-Covid-19 and Hantavirus among them-reveals the profound interdependence of human, animal, and environmental health. At the same time, dominant responses to environmental crises, which made possible the conditions of crisis in the first place, tend to privilege scientific discovery and technological innovation while neglecting the cultural narratives, entrenched biases, and networks of power that shape human-animal relationships.. To that end, imagining more just and hospitable futures requires new interdisciplinary approaches that recognize animals and interspecies relations as critical to collective flourishing and environmental sustainability. The Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium will bring together scholars, artists, students, animal professionals, and community members across the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences to discuss animals and multispecies futures. The symposium is designed not only as a scholarly gathering, but as the start of a long-term collaborative network capable of shaping future research, public humanities work, community partnerships, and environmental dialogue. The inaugural Spring 2027 Symposium will center on the keyword "care," inviting participants to analyze how different disciplines, professions, and communities define and mobilize care in relation to animals, multispecies justice, and environmental stewardship. In doing so, the Symposium will evaluate practices of protection and responsibility alongside the violences and inequalities that shape life across species. For example, how might a humanities scholar, veterinarian, ecologist, or activist understand and practice care differently, and what might each learn from the knowledge, methods, and questions of the others? How might regional, place-based, and communal forms of knowledge offer different ways of understanding our relationships and responsibilities to animals? How is care negotiated when the welfare of an individual animal comes into conflict with the preservation of a population, species, or ecosystem? What might care mean for animals such as insects, whose small size, vast numbers, and frequent classification as pests or disease vectors complicate familiar practices of care? How do animals care for themselves, one another, and members of other species, and what might these practices teach us about caring for each other and the more-than-human world? The Symposium invites participants to consider what becomes possible when different ways of knowing and relating to animals are brought into conversation, and how such exchanges might expand our understanding and practice of care across species.
